pages.description: S.1582 creates federal rules for "stablecoins" — digital coins an issuer must redeem for a fixed dollar value. Only permitted, regulated companies may issue them, and each coin must be fully backed one-to-one by cash or similar safe assets that issuers may not lend out.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.1582?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect The bill sets national rules for stablecoin issuers: companies that promise to redeem digital money for a fixed sum. The rules cover financial backing, repayment and controls on unlawful payments. “This bill establishes a regulatory framework for payment stablecoins (digital assets which an issuer must redeem for a fixed value).” [1]

points.title: It strengthens tools for stopping payments for crimes that destroy nature.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It strengthens tools for stopping payments for crimes that destroy nature.

  • Because Section 4 requires approved issuers to maintain “technical capabilities, policies, and procedures to block, freeze, and reject specific or impermissible transactions that violate Federal or State laws, rules, or regulations” [2].
  • Because Section 8 makes foreign coins’ availability through U.S. trading services depend on obeying lawful orders: “unless the foreign payment stablecoin issuer has the technological capability to comply and complies with the terms of any lawful order.” [2]
  • Because Those orders cover named coins or accounts under federal law. They must be “issued or promulgated under Federal law” [2] and specify “the payment stablecoins or accounts subject to blocking with reasonable particularity” [2].
  • Because Treasury can bar U.S. service providers from trading a foreign issuer’s coins after it defies an order. Section 8 provides for a notice “prohibiting digital asset service providers from facilitating secondary trading of payment stablecoins issued by the foreign payment stablecoin issuer in the United States.” [2]
  • Because Stablecoins provide a payment route for illicit gold. A March 2026 investigation reports: “Some of the gold originating from Guyana is reportedly sold in Venezuela in exchange for Tether, a cryptocurrency stablecoin pegged to the US dollar.” [3]
  • Because Gold mining destroys forests and pollutes soil: “Deforestation due to gold mining wipes out tropical rainforests and contaminates soil with heavy metals” [4].
  • Because Wildlife traffickers also use digital currencies. A conservation practitioners’ forum reports that “criminal networks involved in IWT are increasingly leveraging cryptocurrencies for payments, laundering profits, and facilitating global operations.” [5] IWT means illegal wildlife trade.
  • Because Wildlife trafficking “threatens critical biodiversity, damages fragile ecosystems” [6].
  • Because Financial checks help stop these crimes. FinCEN says suspicious-payment reports and compliance with financial-crime rules “are crucial to identifying and stopping environmental crimes and related money laundering.” [6]
  • Note Existing rules required “customer due diligence, and transaction monitoring of clients” [7]. The bill adds explicit freezing duties and enforceable conditions on foreign issuers’ access to U.S. trading services.
  • So For environmental-crime payments covered by lawful U.S. orders, the bill strengthens the means to interrupt payments and seize proceeds. Giving authorities stronger tools against activities that destroy forests and wildlife serves [NAME]’s wish to defend nature.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Before the vote, Tether reported voluntarily assisting with freezes in over 900 law-enforcement requests over three years, about 460 from U.S. agencies, and reported more than $2.5 billion in frozen USDT. Sources: [8].

Evidence note: The wildlife-trade source discusses cryptocurrencies generally and does not name stablecoins. The gold report's Tether statement is worded 'reportedly' and names no wallets or orders. Sources: [5], [3].

Evidence note: FinCEN and OFAC's April 2026 proposed rule would apply secondary-market obligations to blocking, freezing and rejecting impermissible transactions and to complying with lawful orders. It does not propose requiring issuers, as part of an AML/CFT program, to monitor secondary-market activity or file SARs on secondary-market transactions, and it requests comment. Section 9(d) rulemaking is separate. Sources: [9].

points.title: It better protects donations used to defend forests.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It better protects donations used to defend forests.

  • Because Rainforest Foundation US already accepts USDC donations: “RFUS accepts donations in various popular cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, and USDC.” [10] USDC is a stablecoin: reporting on solar payments identifies it as “the stablecoin USDC” [11].
  • Because This donation route saves money for forest protection: “Crypto donations have lower transaction fees for RFUS than traditional payment methods, enabling more funds to go directly to rainforest protection and supporting Indigenous communities.” [10]
  • Because It also lets donors follow their transfers, giving them “the ability to track contributions in real time.” [10]
  • Because The bill requires full backing for approved coins: “Issuers would be required to hold at least one dollar of permitted reserves for every one dollar of stablecoins issued.” [12]
  • Because Section 11 puts coin holders first in line for repayment from required reserves if an issuer fails. Their claims rank “over the claims of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and any other holder of claims against the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, with respect to required payment stablecoin reserves” [2].
  • Because The bill keeps required reserves outside the pool used to pay an issuer’s other debts in bankruptcy. It “amends Section 541 of the Bankruptcy Code to exclude stablecoin reserves from property of the bankruptcy estate” [13].
  • Because This protection applies only while a gift remains a stablecoin. RFUS reports that it “immediately exchanges most of the crypto donations it receives for US dollars.” [10] Coverage therefore reaches USDC gifts during processing and any share not exchanged at once.
  • So The lower fees and tracking already existed; the bill’s addition is protection for gifts while held as approved stablecoins. These rules reduce the risk that issuer failure or other debts divert those gifts. Protecting this way to give preserves money for forest defence and helps [NAME] take part in defending nature.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: RFUS's reported long-term reserve initiative is a Bitcoin Treasury, which is not a payment stablecoin. Its lower fees and tracking were reported in December 2024. Sources: [10].

points.title: It opens a clearer legal path to faster payments for renewable electricity.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It opens a clearer legal path to faster payments for renewable electricity.

  • Because Section 16 gives firms under federal banking regulators clear permission to handle stablecoins: they “are authorized to engage in the payment stablecoin activities and investments contemplated by this Act” [2].
  • Because Legal uncertainty held back use. Environmental-market operator Innovo describes institutional stablecoin payments as “something many were reluctant to do without legal clarity.” [14]
  • Because Innovo already uses stablecoins in its energy markets: “At Innovo, we built stablecoin settlement directly into our digital infrastructure, so all energy transactions on our platform experience a new way of settlement and finance.” [14]
  • Because These trades include credits for renewable electricity: “Whether you're trading renewable energy credits, settling transactions in energy markets, or moving carbon offsets, stablecoins offer a functioning and faster modern market than legacy systems.” [14]
  • Because Faster payment releases money tied up during trades. Innovo explains: “When you’re not locking up funds for days at a time, you can put that money to work elsewhere, sooner.” [14]
  • Because Innovo directs this point to clean-energy participants, naming “a corporate energy buyer, a project developer, or an institution active in clean energy markets” [14].
  • Because Solar projects already use this payment method. Fortune reports: “Owners of each farm receive the stablecoin USDC for the production of Glow carbon credits” [11].
  • Because Glow’s stated funding model targets projects needing help to get built: “Glow seeks out solar farms that are borderline viable and gives them just barely enough money to get them over the line for construction” [11].
  • Because Renewable electricity helps cut climate pollution. A U.S. energy-lab review finds that “total life cycle GHG emissions from renewables and nuclear energy are much lower and generally less variable than those from fossil fuels.” [15] This comparison counts gases that warm the climate over the equipment’s whole life.
  • So The bill’s clear rules help institutions use faster payments in renewable-energy markets. Releasing money sooner modestly improves the finances of participants in those markets, including developers, and the solar example shows that some projects operate near the edge of viability. This inference does not specify an amount of new renewable power. Making this finance easier to use serves [NAME]’s wish to protect nature from pollution.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: OCC said in January 2021 that national banks and federal savings associations may use stablecoins for payment activities, and in March 2025 rescinded its supervisory nonobjection requirement. Innovo's July 2025 article says it had 'already operationalized' stablecoin settlement. Sources: [16], [17], [14].

Evidence note: A report prepared for EPA's Green Power Partnership says REC purchases verify that renewable energy was generated and used, not that new capacity was deployed, and that a unit of voluntary demand cannot generally be mapped to an additional unit of generation on a 1:1 basis. It adds that voluntary demand serves market functions that should affect supply decisions, and it describes tight developer margins. Innovo's article says freed money can go 'elsewhere', without naming a destination. Fortune attributes Glow's construction money to crypto or private equity investors, and Glow says its USDC pool is funded by electricity revenue. Sources: [18], [14], [11], [19].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose S.1582?
directions.main_effect_html:
Main effect The bill creates national rules for stablecoins—digital tokens redeemable for a set amount of money. CRS states: “This bill establishes a regulatory framework for payment stablecoins (digital assets which an issuer must redeem for a fixed value).” [1]

  • Because Under the rules in force before the bill, uncertainty had deterred major banks: “major banks and other traditional financial institutions largely stayed away from them, put off by regulatory uncertainty and crypto’s association with illicit transactions.” [20]
  • Because Section 16 expressly opens the business to regulated firms: “Entities regulated by the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators are authorized to engage in the payment stablecoin activities and investments contemplated by this Act” [2]. This gives firms a clear legal basis for taking part.
  • Because Stablecoins support crypto trading. Brookings reported in May 2025: “Stablecoins currently are used mainly for trading crypto assets” [21]. A study also found that “stablecoins increase the trading volume of Bitcoin.” [22]
  • Because Bitcoin’s value affects the rewards for mining—the computer work that earns coins. The White House science office explains: “As a crypto-asset becomes more valuable, the mining rewards also become more valuable. This attracts more miners and computing resources to solve the cryptographic math problem.” [23]
  • Because Earthjustice clean-energy attorney Mandy DeRoche connects the bill’s wider acceptance of crypto to mining growth: “The more that crypto currency generally is legitimized and used, the more crypto mining there will be” [24].
  • So The bill encourages mining by expanding and legitimizing a trading channel for Bitcoin. This increases exposure to the environmental harms below.
  • Note Running stablecoins on low-energy networks leaves their role in Bitcoin trading intact. Bitcoin “can only be created through mining” [25]; its mining rewards still attract computing power as its value grows.

points.title: Encouraging mining adds climate pollution that damages forests and other ecosystems.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Encouraging mining adds climate pollution that damages forests and other ecosystems.

  • Because Mining responds to financial rewards with real emissions. At Pennsylvania’s Scrubgrass coal plant, which supplies an on-site Bitcoin mine, researchers found that “carbon emissions respond swiftly to mining incentives” [26].
  • Because The risk extends to electricity bought from the grid. The White House report explains that “coal and natural gas often supply electricity generation for each additional unit of electricity demanded in the United States.” [23]
  • Because Buying existing renewable power that other users would consume can shift greenhouse gas (GHG) pollution to those users. The report explains: “When a crypto-asset mine purchases electricity from existing renewable sources, it displaces the GHG emissions in the near-term, shifting users of renewable sources to fossil fuel sources.” [23]
  • Because Climate damage includes “loss of forests, homes, and infrastructure from increasing wildfires” [23].
  • So The bill encourages an activity whose added power demand worsens climate risks. Protecting forests and ecosystems gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that expansion.
points.con_html:
Response The climate claim skips the step from more stablecoin trading to higher Bitcoin mining rewards.

  • Because The trading study finds that “stablecoins increase the trading volume of Bitcoin.” [22] Trading volume measures how much changes hands, not how much Bitcoin’s price rises.
  • Because The mining report explains the price link: “As a crypto-asset becomes more valuable, the mining rewards also become more valuable. This attracts more miners and computing resources to solve the cryptographic math problem.” [23]
  • Because A 2018 study’s model separates trading from price gains: “Tether issuances do not impact subsequent Bitcoin returns, however, they do impact traded volumes.” [27] Returns here means price gains or losses.
  • Because A 2020 study of Tether flows to exchanges also reports: “We find no significant effect on the prices of Bitcoin and Ethereum” [28]. The authors add that their aggregate results “do not discount the possibility that price manipulation can occur” [28].
  • Because The coal-plant study tests a price change: “We exploit daily variation in Bitcoin price as a natural experiment for an 86 megawatt coal-fired power plant with on-site cryptomining.” [26]
  • So The trading-volume finding does not establish the price rise that links the bill to the coal plant’s added emissions. The grid and renewable-power arguments also start with added mining power demand; they do not establish that S.1582 would cause it.

Shared objection The PRO’s claim about wider crypto acceptance overlooks how stablecoin trades reach Bitcoin miners.

  • Because Section 16 authorizes stablecoin business: “Entities regulated by the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators are authorized to engage in the payment stablecoin activities and investments contemplated by this Act” [2]. That permission does not itself establish increased Bitcoin buying.
  • Because Stablecoins also serve people selling Bitcoin. The 2020 study describes investors “liquidating their Bitcoin holdings” [28] into Tether during a price crash.
  • Because Miners receive transaction fees for entries in Bitcoin’s shared record: they collect “fees associated with transactions within the block.” [23]
  • Because Exchange trading is different: “centralized crypto-asset trading platforms typically use off-chain transactions” [23]—trades recorded within the platform rather than in Bitcoin’s shared record.
  • So Trading volume counts activity that includes Bitcoin sales and trades that pay no Bitcoin block fee. It does not measure a rise in Bitcoin prices or fees paid to miners.
  • Because The PRO’s remaining bridge is DeRoche’s forecast: “The more that crypto currency generally is legitimized and used, the more crypto mining there will be” [24].
  • So That broad forecast does not resolve the evidence separating trading growth from price gains or show that the bill would raise miner fees. Legal permission and wider stablecoin use therefore do not establish the extra mining on which all seven reasons depend.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The cited price-null studies analyze Tether issuance or flows in samples ending by 2020 and do not study legal recognition. The price-emissions study covers one 86 MW Pennsylvania coal plant, and the OSTP report dates from 2022. Sources: [28], [27], [26].

points.pro_html:
Point 2 Encouraging mining adds air pollution that harms forests and lakes.

  • Because The Scrubgrass study also found more nitrogen oxides, polluting gases from burning fuel: “We find that nitrogen oxide pollutants increase with higher Bitcoin prices” [26].
  • Because These gases help form acid rain. EPA explains that they “interact with water, oxygen and other chemicals in the atmosphere to form acid rain. Acid rain harms sensitive ecosystems such as lakes and forests.” [29]
  • So Mining’s air pollution threatens nature beyond its climate effects. [NAME] has a reason to oppose expanding this source of damage to forests and lakes.
points.con_html:
Response The air-pollution claim also relies on a Bitcoin price rise that the PRO’s stablecoin evidence does not establish.

  • Because The coal-plant study reports: “We find that nitrogen oxide pollutants increase with higher Bitcoin prices” [26].
  • Because EPA explains the later harm: “Acid rain harms sensitive ecosystems such as lakes and forests.” [29]
  • So These sources connect higher Bitcoin prices to harmful pollution. They supply no link from S.1582’s stablecoin rules to those higher prices or added mining emissions.

points.title: Encouraging mining increases pressure on scarce freshwater.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Encouraging mining increases pressure on scarce freshwater.

  • Because Mining consumes water through cooling and electricity production. A study explains that “water consumption refers to the portion of water that becomes unavailable for reuse after withdrawal, primarily due to evaporation in cooling systems.” [30] Its measure covers “the freshwater consumed due to both direct and indirect water consumption during the operational stage of Bitcoin mining devices.” [30]
  • Because This demand reaches water-stressed areas. Brookings identifies mining’s water risks “especially in drought-prone or resource-scarce areas” [31].
  • So Expanding mining adds demand for a limited natural resource. Protecting scarce freshwater gives [NAME] a separate reason to oppose that expansion.
points.con_html:
Response Bitcoin’s water footprint does not establish that the bill would add freshwater demand.

  • Because For cooling at mining sites, the water study states: “Water usage depends on cooling system types and local climate conditions.” [30]
  • Because For electricity production, it states: “To determine the indirect water footprint, it is important to establish the power demand of the network and the power sources.” [30]
  • So Added water demand requires a change in mining’s cooling or power use. Greater trading volume establishes neither. The warning about water scarcity does not show that S.1582 would increase that demand.

points.title: Encouraging mining threatens fish and water quality through power-plant cooling.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Encouraging mining threatens fish and water quality through power-plant cooling.

  • Because Plants supplying mines with once-through cooling take water from rivers or lakes and return it heated, with cleaning chemicals. The withdrawal and discharge “can harm fish and wildlife, and can negatively impact recreation and water quality” [23].
  • So Expanding mining increases exposure to damage from taking and returning cooling water. Protecting wildlife and waterways gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
points.con_html:
Response The cooling-water evidence does not show that stablecoin rules would increase harm to fish or waterways.

  • Because The report identifies the source of harm: “Fossil-fired electricity that directly powers mining operations also impacts local water.” [23]
  • Because At plants that take river or lake water for cooling and return it heated, withdrawals and discharges “can harm fish and wildlife, and can negatively impact recreation and water quality.” [23]
  • So This path requires added use of those power plants and cooling systems. The PRO has not connected stablecoin trading to that increase, so it has not established added harm from the bill.

points.title: Encouraging mining creates more discarded equipment that can pollute air and water.

Point 6 Encouraging mining creates more discarded equipment that can pollute air and water.

  • Because Dedicated mining chips have limited reuse and are regularly replaced: “Currently, ASICs cannot be used for any other purpose, so companies often discard, sell, or reduce the use of older generations of ASICs after approximately one year and four months.” [23]

  • So Expanding mining adds equipment that becomes waste and raises pollution risks when poorly disposed of. Protecting nature from that pollution gives [NAME] another reason to oppose the expansion.

Response The equipment’s short life does not show that S.1582 would add discarded mining machines.

  • So This explains how mining equipment becomes waste. The PRO still needs to establish that the bill would add machines to that replacement cycle. The cycle and the danger of poor disposal supply no such link.

points.title: Encouraging mining spreads noise that puts nearby wildlife at risk.

Point 7 Encouraging mining spreads noise that puts nearby wildlife at risk.

  • Because Mining sites reach rural areas: “Many of the mines are sited in small towns and rural areas.” [24]

In an experiment playing gas-compressor noise, researchers found that “Eastern Bluebirds and Tree Swallows nesting in noisy nest boxes spent less time incubating their eggs, had fewer eggs hatch, and produced fewer young than their neighbors nesting in quiet boxes.” [32]
  • So More noisy mining sites add a risk to wildlife in surrounding habitats. [NAME]’s wish to defend nature gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that expansion.
points.con_html:
Response The noise experiment does not establish extra wildlife exposure caused by S.1582.

  • Because The mining report identifies an existing noise source: “Air-cooled mining computers contain high-velocity fans that can generate noise pollution.” [23]
  • Because The bird study tested compressor noise: “we experimentally introduced compressor noise without associated changes to the physical environment.” [32]
  • So Existing rural mines and harm from compressor noise do not establish that stablecoin rules would add mining sites, fan noise, or wildlife exposed to it. The bill-to-harm link remains missing.

pages.description: S.1582 creates federal rules for "stablecoins" — digital coins an issuer must redeem for a fixed dollar value. Only permitted, regulated companies may issue them, and each coin must be fully backed one-to-one by cash or similar safe assets that issuers may not lend out.
