directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.1582?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with law in force on July 17, 2025, the bill adds a U.S. licensing system and common safeguards for payment stablecoins, digital tokens redeemable for a fixed amount of money. “This bill establishes a regulatory framework for payment stablecoins (digital assets which an issuer must redeem for a fixed value).” [1] The existing system lacked common federal rules: “the United States has operated without a clear Federal framework for dollar-backed payment stablecoins” [2].

points.title: Required backing protects money that people with little financial cushion need for essentials.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Required backing protects money that people with little financial cushion need for essentials.

  • Because Issuers licensed under the bill must “maintain identifiable reserves backing the outstanding payment stablecoins of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer on an at least 1 to 1 basis” [3]. The backing must cover at least the full amount users are owed.
  • Because The permitted backing includes cash and short-term U.S. government debt: “The bill would limit permitted reserves to coins and currency, deposits held at insured banks and credit unions, short-dated Treasury bills” [4].
  • Because Reuse is limited to listed reserve-investment, custody, and cash-out needs. Outside those purposes, reserves “may not be pledged, rehypothecated, or reused by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, either directly or indirectly” [3].
  • Because Safe, readily available backing supports repayment: “they need to be backed by safe and liquid assets, like cash, Treasury bills, and central bank reserves, so they can offer convertibility at par.” [5]
  • Because Ordinary crypto users are less able to absorb losses: “most retail participants lack the resources, information, and financial resilience needed to navigate this volatile space.” [6]
  • Because Dollar-linked coins also serve people facing unstable currencies: “Stablecoins can also mitigate local currency and inflationary risks, major advantages in volatile markets.” [7]
  • Because Aid recipients already use them. UNHCR “successfully executed a small pilot to distribute cash assistance to a group of people displaced by the war in Ukraine in Circle Internet Financial’s USD Coin (USDC)” [8].
  • So Enforceable backing rules protect against coins issued without enough money to repay users. That protects small savings and aid payments, including money vulnerable people abroad need for food, shelter, and care.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Before the vote, Circle described full, liquid and unencumbered reserves and monthly third-party assurance. New York's guidance required full backing, timely par redemption and public CPA reports for stablecoins under its supervision, and New York licensing rules required cyber programs and background reports. New York rules applied only to New York-supervised issuers. Sources: [9], [10], [11].

points.title: Cash-out rules and advance fee notices protect people who depend on ready access to their money.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Cash-out rules and advance fee notices protect people who depend on ready access to their money.

  • Because Issuers must publish procedures for “timely redemption of outstanding payment stablecoins” [3]. Discretionary limits require a regulator's decision: “any discretionary limitations on timely redemptions can only be imposed by a State qualified payment stablecoin regulator, the Corporation, the Comptroller, or the Board” [3].
  • Because Purchase and cash-out fees must be disclosed in plain language, and “such fees can only be changed upon not less than 7 days' prior notice to consumers” [3].
  • So Issuers lose the freedom to impose their own discretionary cash-out limits or change fees without warning. This protects people whose essential spending leaves little room for delays or surprise charges.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO leaves out the link between issuer cash-out terms and the terms governing access to spending money held through other firms.

  • Because Section 4 regulates “the issuer's redemption policy” [3] and requires that “such fees can only be changed upon not less than 7 days' prior notice to consumers” [3]. This notice sits within the issuer's duty.
  • Because Circle's pre-vote prospectus explains: “Transactions between third parties may be subject to fees charged by the parties to the transaction or the secondary marketplace on which the transaction occurs.” [9] Those fees and terms “are governed by agreements between the parties to the transactions and/or the rules of the secondary marketplace” [9].
  • So This response does not dispute the protection for people who redeem directly with an issuer. It challenges the wider step: the issuer's notice does not govern every wallet, exchange, or cash-pickup firm's charges and delays, and the PRO has not shown how the change improves access for households relying on those firms.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Before the vote, Circle described full, liquid and unencumbered reserves and monthly third-party assurance. New York's guidance required full backing, timely par redemption and public CPA reports for stablecoins under its supervision, and New York licensing rules required cyber programs and background reports. New York rules applied only to New York-supervised issuers. Sources: [9], [10], [11].

points.title: Checked reports and truthful marketing protect people who cannot investigate a financial firm themselves.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Checked reports and truthful marketing protect people who cannot investigate a financial firm themselves.

  • Because Issuers must “publish the monthly composition of the issuer's reserves on the website of the issuer” [3]. Monthly reports must be “examined by a registered public accounting firm.” [3]
  • Because Senior executives must submit “a certification as to the accuracy of the monthly report” [3]. This makes named managers answer for the information users receive.
  • Because The bill bans false claims of government backing or insurance: “It shall be unlawful to represent that payment stablecoins are backed by the full faith and credit of the United States, guaranteed by the United States Government, or subject to Federal deposit insurance or Federal share insurance.” [3]
  • Because Such deception harms people relying on savings. Brookings describes Celsius customers misled about safety or insurance: “Many victims had invested their retirement savings or emergency funds.” [6]
  • So Public reports, outside checks, and marketing rules make accurate safety information less dependent on a customer's expertise or wealth. That gives people [NAME] does not know fairer treatment when deciding whom to trust with their money.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO's Celsius example does not show the added protection it is used to illustrate.

  • Because The cited harm concerns “major crypto platforms such as Celsius and Voyager” [6]. A report about a coin issuer's reserves is not a report about a separate platform's ability to return its customers' money.
  • Because The FDIC stated in 2022: “The Federal Deposit Insurance Act (FDI Act) prohibits any person from representing or implying that an uninsured product is FDIC–insured or from knowingly misrepresenting the extent and manner of deposit insurance.” [12] The deposit-insurance part of the bill's marketing ban therefore overlaps an existing prohibition.
  • So This leaves the bill's reserve reports, executive certifications, and ban on claims of U.S. government backing unanswered. The Celsius example does not establish how those provisions relieve customers of judging the safety of a separate platform holding their savings.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Before the vote, Circle described full, liquid and unencumbered reserves and monthly third-party assurance. New York's guidance required full backing, timely par redemption and public CPA reports for stablecoins under its supervision, and New York licensing rules required cyber programs and background reports. New York rules applied only to New York-supervised issuers. Sources: [9], [10], [11].

points.title: Customer ownership and repayment priority protect users when a firm fails.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Customer ownership and repayment priority protect users when a firm fails.

  • Because Section 10 sets customer-ownership duties for covered firms holding backing assets, coins pledged for debts, or keys used to issue coins: “as belonging to such customer and not as the property of such person” [3].
  • Because Its default separation rule requires customer assets to be “segregated from and not be commingled with the assets of the person.” [3]
  • Because Customers' claims to coins held by those firms rank ahead of other creditors, unless the customer expressly agrees otherwise: “the claims of the customer against such person with respect to such payment stablecoins shall have priority” [3].
  • Because In an issuer's failure, holders have first claim to required reserves, shared in proportion to their claims: “the claim of a person holding payment stablecoins issued by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer shall have priority, on a ratable basis with the claims of other persons holding such payment stablecoins” [3].
  • Because Unpaid coin claims also receive “first priority over any other claim” [3] against the issuer's remaining assets, to the extent the issuer failed to hold legally required reserves.
  • Because In a court case to reorganize an issuer, a regulator “shall raise, and shall appear and be heard on, any issue, including the protection of customers” [3].
  • So Users gain protection against unrelated business debts, a proportionate share of reserves, and a public voice in the issuer's failure. These rules support just treatment of customers who lack the power to bargain for protection themselves.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO's failure protection does not reach Treasury backing that a lender can take first.

  • Because Section 4 permits using Treasury reserves as collateral for borrowing to meet redemptions: “creating liquidity to meet reasonable expectations of requests to redeem payment stablecoins” [3]. Brookings explains the effect of these secured loans, called repurchase agreements: in bankruptcy, “the repo lender could seize the Treasury collateral if the stablecoin issuer could not return the cash.” [13]
  • Because In that event, “assets in segregated accounts would fall short of what is needed for 1:1 redemption.” [13] A right to share those assets does not restore the seized collateral.
  • So This leaves the protection against other business debts unanswered. It challenges the PRO's description of holders' claim to a full proportionate share of reserves where backing has been pledged in this way.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Before the vote, Circle described full, liquid and unencumbered reserves and monthly third-party assurance. New York's guidance required full backing, timely par redemption and public CPA reports for stablecoins under its supervision, and New York licensing rules required cyber programs and background reports. New York rules applied only to New York-supervised issuers. Sources: [9], [10], [11].

points.title: Required safeguards for issuers' computer systems address theft and payment failures.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Required safeguards for issuers' computer systems address theft and payment failures.

  • Because These risks threaten users' money: “Stablecoins could fall victim to a cyberattack, with hackers draining funds or manipulating token issuances.” [7]
  • Because Section 4 directs federal regulators to set “appropriate operational, compliance, and information technology risk management principles-based requirements and standards” [3].
  • So Requiring issuers to manage these risks adds protection against theft and disrupted payments. That matters especially for people with few resources to replace lost money or wait for a failed payment system to recover.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Before the vote, Circle described full, liquid and unencumbered reserves and monthly third-party assurance. New York's guidance required full backing, timely par redemption and public CPA reports for stablecoins under its supervision, and New York licensing rules required cyber programs and background reports. New York rules applied only to New York-supervised issuers. Sources: [9], [10], [11].

Evidence note: The FTC's December 2024 guide says covered financial institutions, including check cashers and wire transferors, must maintain an information security program. Sources: [14].

points.title: Screening managers and public enforcement protect customers from misconduct.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 Screening managers and public enforcement protect customers from misconduct.

  • Because The bill excludes managers convicted of specified crimes: “The bill would prohibit anyone who has been convicted of certain financial crimes of being an officer or director of an issuer.” [4]
  • Because Federal licensing reviews must assess “The competence, experience, and integrity of the officers, directors, and principal shareholders of the applicant” [3].
  • Because Federal regulators can order a violating issuer to “take affirmative action to correct the conditions resulting from any such violation or practice.” [3] State regulators receive “supervisory, examination, and enforcement authority over all State qualified payment stablecoin issuers of such State.” [3]
  • So Public officials must check managers and gain powers to correct misconduct. Customers receive protection that does not depend on their own money or skill in investigating and challenging a firm.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO's statement that public officials must check managers leaves out the bill's approval route without a completed decision.

  • Because Section 5 sets the decision deadline at “Not later than 120 days after receiving a substantially complete application under subsection (a)” [3]. If the regulator misses the specified deadline, “the application shall be deemed approved.” [3]
  • So A missed deadline can produce approval without a completed review of the managers. This leaves the conviction bar and enforcement powers unanswered; it challenges only the claim that officials' licensing review always takes place.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Before the vote, Circle described full, liquid and unencumbered reserves and monthly third-party assurance. New York's guidance required full backing, timely par redemption and public CPA reports for stablecoins under its supervision, and New York licensing rules required cyber programs and background reports. New York rules applied only to New York-supervised issuers. Sources: [9], [10], [11].

points.title: Checks on wider financial risks protect people who never use stablecoins.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 Checks on wider financial risks protect people who never use stablecoins.

  • Because A major crypto failure, including a stablecoin issuer's collapse, “could affect pensions, savings, small business loans, and more.” [6]
  • Because Section 6 requires examinations of federally supervised issuers for risks to “the stability of the financial system of the United States” [3] and checks their systems for controlling those risks.
  • Because Section 4 requires federal rules on “reserve asset diversification, including deposit concentration at banking institutions, and interest rate risk management standards” [3]. These address reliance on one bank and losses from changing interest rates.
  • So The bill directs oversight at routes through which issuer trouble can spread to other financial firms. Protecting pensions, savings, and credit from those risks extends [NAME]'s concern to strangers who never chose to use stablecoins.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Before the vote, Circle described full, liquid and unencumbered reserves and monthly third-party assurance. New York's guidance required full backing, timely par redemption and public CPA reports for stablecoins under its supervision, and New York licensing rules required cyber programs and background reports. New York rules applied only to New York-supervised issuers. Sources: [9], [10], [11].

Evidence note: CRS states the bill exempts issuers from bank regulatory capital standards while requiring tailored capital rules. Brookings states liquidity and diversification requirements are not sufficient substitutes for capital requirements. Sources: [4], [15].

points.title: Required controls on criminal funds protect victims and help preserve stolen money for recovery.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 Required controls on criminal funds protect victims and help preserve stolen money for recovery.

  • Because Tether's coins appear in criminal cases: “Its USDT coins have been seized and forfeited in cases involving fraud, terrorist financing, sanctions violations and other criminal activity.” [16]
  • Because Section 4 requires suspicious-transaction reporting and capabilities to “block, freeze, and reject specific or impermissible transactions that violate Federal or State laws, rules, or regulations” [3]. Section 5 requires compliance programs aimed in particular at “cartels and organizations designated as foreign terrorist organizations” [3].
  • Because Section 8 conditions U.S. trading through digital asset service providers on a foreign issuer having “the technological capability to comply and complies with the terms of any lawful order.” [3]
  • Because Freezing and seizing proceeds serves victims. In a crypto-fraud case, the U.S. Secret Service described work to “identify victims and seize these funds so that they can eventually be returned to their rightful owners.” [17]
  • So Requiring issuers to detect and block criminal transfers makes it harder to move stolen funds beyond recovery or use them to finance further harm. This serves justice for victims across borders, including people [NAME] will never meet.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO's inference about detecting criminal transfers leaves out a monitoring limit on issuer duties.

  • Because Identifying criminal transfers is a separate task from freezing funds once identified. CRS warns: “It is unclear, however, how issuers could address their BSA/AML monitoring responsibilities once stablecoins are off-ramped to pseudonymous public blockchains, which are not subject to issuer controls.” [18] These networks use digital addresses rather than verified names.
  • Because FinCEN's April 2026 proposed rule says: “FinCEN is not proposing to require a PPSI as part of an AML/CFT program to monitor secondary market activity” [19]. It also proposes no duty “to file SARs on secondary market transactions” [19]. This is a proposal, open to comment.
  • So This leaves the freezing capability and the condition on foreign issuers unanswered. It challenges the PRO's inference that duties placed on issuers will detect criminal transfers that move away from their direct customers.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: FinCEN clarified in 2013 that AML/CFT reporting requirements apply to crypto transmission. DOJ's cited recovery case was announced on June 18, 2025, and thanks Tether for its proactive assistance. Sources: [20], [17].

Evidence note: FinCEN and OFAC's April 2026 proposed rule would apply secondary-market obligations to blocking, freezing and rejecting impermissible transactions and to complying with lawful orders. It does not propose requiring issuers, as part of an AML/CFT program, to monitor secondary-market activity or file SARs on secondary-market transactions, and it requests comment. Section 9(d) rulemaking is separate. Sources: [19].

points.title: Rules against forced purchases and blocking rivals protect customers from unfair terms.
points.pro_html:
Point 9 Rules against forced purchases and blocking rivals protect customers from unfair terms.

  • Because An issuer may not condition service on buying “an additional paid product or service from the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, or any of its subsidiaries” [3] or on agreeing “to not obtain an additional product or service from a competitor.” [3]
  • So Customers gain protection against unwanted extra costs and pressure to give up other providers. That is fairer treatment of people with limited money and gives competing businesses a fairer chance to serve them.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Under existing antitrust law, tying liability generally depends on market power; the FTC general counsel described exclusive dealing as potentially procompetitive or anticompetitive. Sources: [21], [22].

points.title: Limits on commercial use of payment data give customers a say over firms' use of their private financial lives.
points.pro_html:
Point 10 Limits on commercial use of payment data give customers a say over firms' use of their private financial lives.

  • Because For public companies mainly engaged outside finance, approval to issue coins requires consent limits on using customers' private transaction data: “unless the public company receives consent from the consumer, nonpublic personal information obtained from stablecoin transaction data may not be-- (aa) used to target, personalize, or rank advertising or other content; (bb) sold to any third party; or (cc) shared with non- affiliates” [3].
  • So Requiring permission stops these firms from taking those commercial benefits from private payment histories without customers' agreement. Giving customers a say in that bargain supports just treatment.
points.con_html:
Response Requiring permission does not by itself establish the just treatment the PRO infers from a customer's agreement.

  • Because For the public companies it covers, Section 4 allows the listed commercial data uses if “the public company receives consent from the consumer” [3]. The paragraph sets no requirement that the service remain available when the consumer refuses those uses.
  • Because The separate ban on forced purchases concerns “an additional paid product or service” [3]. Agreement to data use is not an additional paid product.
  • So This provision alone does not rule out making agreement a condition of service. The PRO needs a reason why obtaining that agreement gives customers fair control over their private payment histories; the word consent does not supply it.

points.title: A nationwide licensing route widens opportunity for new providers and the people they serve.
points.pro_html:
Point 11 A nationwide licensing route widens opportunity for new providers and the people they serve.

  • Because Repeated state licensing creates a barrier for nonbank payment firms: “the time and cost of obtaining such licenses can be daunting for Fintechs” [23].
  • Because Section 5 replaces extra state licensing for federally approved issuers. Its provisions “supersede and preempt any State requirement for a charter, license, or other authorization to do business” [3] for those issuers.
  • Because Both banks and nonbanks can apply: “Stablecoins could be issued by banks and credit unions (through subsidiaries) or nonbanks.” [4] Public networks remain eligible: “The issuance of a payment stablecoin on an open, public, or decentralized network shall not be a valid ground for denial of an application received under subsection (a).” [3]
  • Because This matters for access: “Stablecoins enable users to save in a stable currency and transact globally without a bank account” [24].
  • Because Stablecoins already offer useful transfer options: “Where permitted, stablecoins offer a faster and cheaper alternative to traditional remittance solutions. This is especially important for migrant workers and in solving perennial small business challenges.” [25]
  • Because The stakes reach vulnerable households. The Dallas Fed describes money sent home to Mexico: “These remittances are a valuable lifeline for millions of households in Mexico, especially in the poorest states.” [26]
  • Because Smaller firms also face barriers that these services address: stablecoins can “widen access to trade and finance for smaller companies that struggle with correspondent banking.” [24] Correspondent banking means banks using other banks to handle international payments.
  • So Removing repeated licensing gives new providers a fairer chance to offer these services nationwide under the bill's safeguards. This lowers a barrier to serving people who need bankless payments or lower-cost international transfers, including migrant families and small firms. That advances equal financial opportunity beyond established banks and their customers.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Dallas Fed article says stablecoin transfers remain subject to other fees and require digital and financial literacy. The K&L Gates remittance example still uses a licensed foreign agent or app for pickup and notes that states may keep other requirements short of a license. Sources: [26], [23].

points.title: Clear approval criteria and appeals require fair treatment of new applicants.
points.pro_html:
Point 12 Clear approval criteria and appeals require fair treatment of new applicants.

  • Because Federal regulators may deny a complete application only on safety grounds: “the activities of the applicant would be unsafe or unsound based on the factors described in subsection (c).” [3]
  • Because A denial must identify shortcomings and offer “actionable recommendations on how the applicant could address the identified material shortcomings.” [3]
  • Because Applicants can request a hearing to challenge rejection: “Regulators would have to justify denials and permit applicants to appeal.” [4]
  • So People seeking to start a qualified provider gain stated criteria, reasons for rejection, and a way to challenge mistakes. This supports [NAME]'s concern for just treatment by public officials.
points.con_html:
Response Procedures for a new federal approval power do not establish fairer treatment than the law they replace.

  • Because The bill makes U.S. issuance by someone without its permission unlawful: “It shall be unlawful for any person other than a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to issue a payment stablecoin in the United States.” [3] Its internal appeal reviews decisions under that new permission requirement.
  • So The stated criteria, reasons and appeal rules constrain a licensing power the bill itself creates. The PRO has not established that applicants receive less arbitrary treatment than under the law in force on July 17, 2025.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Federal law already required a brief statement of grounds for agency denials, with exceptions, and judicial review for legal wrongs from agency action; New York's route had public standards. Sources: [27], [28], [11].

points.title: The ban on issuer-paid interest blocks one incentive to pull deposits away from community lending.
points.pro_html:
Point 13 The ban on issuer-paid interest blocks one incentive to pull deposits away from community lending.

  • Because Section 4 bars issuers from paying holders interest or other returns just for holding or using a coin: “No permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer shall pay the holder of any payment stablecoin any form of interest or yield” [3].
  • Because Issuer-paid interest can attract money banks use to lend: “It also could draw funds away from bank deposits that underpin lending to households and businesses and are a key transmission channel for monetary policy.” [5]
  • Because Deposit losses threaten credit in places with few lending options: “This impact will be especially acute in rural and low-income areas” [29].
  • So The ban prevents issuers from using direct interest payments to draw those deposits. Blocking that incentive protects a source of loans for households and small firms in communities where limited credit already restricts opportunity.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The PPI lending warning builds on a $6.6 trillion figure that CRS and the Treasury advisory presentation describe as at risk or hypothetical. CEA's April 2026 baseline estimates that eliminating stablecoin yield would raise bank lending by $2.1 billion (0.02%), with $500 million from community banks (0.026%). Sources: [30], [31], [32].

Evidence note: CRS reports that much retail stablecoin use occurs through exchanges, that GENIUS does not explicitly prevent exchanges from paying rewards on coins they hold, that many do, and that Circle pays part of its reserve interest to Coinbase. CRS also says the issuer is prohibited from paying interest in a direct issuer-to-customer model, that the restriction would presumably apply to self-custody, and that 'holder' is undefined. Coinbase attributes part of its USDC balance growth to its rewards program. AAF says issuers can effectively circumvent the ban through exchanges or third parties. Sources: [30], [33], [34].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose S.1582?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect The bill creates national rules for issuing payment stablecoins—private digital tokens redeemable for a fixed amount of money: “This bill establishes a regulatory framework for payment stablecoins (digital assets which an issuer must redeem for a fixed value).” [1]. It encourages wider use by removing a barrier to entry: the administration says it “removes regulatory uncertainty that has hindered innovation and competitiveness in the digital assets sector.” [35]. Major banks had “largely stayed away from them, put off by regulatory uncertainty and crypto’s association with illicit transactions.” [36].

points.title: Moving household money into stablecoins exposes essential savings to uninsured losses.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Moving household money into stablecoins exposes essential savings to uninsured losses.

  • Because Replacing an insured bank balance with tokens removes the insurance on that money: stablecoins are “not federally insured” [4].
  • Because The backing can itself lose value: “the permissible reserve assets include uninsured deposits in banks and shares of credit unions” [13]; “uninsured deposits are risky and illiquid” [13].
  • Because The bill also permits borrowing against Treasury securities held as backing. If the issuer cannot repay that loan, the lender can take those securities first: “assets in segregated accounts would fall short of what is needed for 1:1 redemption.” [13].
  • So Expanding this substitute for bank savings exposes people to losing money needed for daily life. Protecting households that cannot replace those losses gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that expansion.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Brookings cautions against overstating stablecoin volumes: without interest, holders have incentives to minimize their holdings, and faster payments let a given volume of stablecoins support more payments. The same paper describes these coins as a substitute for cash or bank transaction accounts. CRS says depositors who shift lose federal insurance, a risk exposure some consumers may not be aware of. Sources: [37], [30].

points.title: Bankruptcy can block access to payment money even when backing assets remain.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Bankruptcy can block access to payment money even when backing assets remain.

  • Because For a nonbank issuer in bankruptcy, withdrawals from those assets are frozen: “Section 11(c) of the proposed Act applies the automatic stay to actions against the reserves.” [38].
  • Because The bill provides “an accelerated procedure for stablecoin holders to obtain relief from the automatic stay” [38], but sets no firm deadline for completing repayment: “the court shall use best efforts to enter a final order to begin distributions under this paragraph not later than 14 days after the date of the required hearing.” [3].
  • So Having assets available is different from having money available to pay for food or rent. Promoting payment money that can remain frozen, even for a shortened period, exposes people without a cash cushion to missed necessities, giving [NAME] a reason to protect them.
points.con_html:
Response The bankruptcy passages do not show that the bill's own bankruptcy rules add a loss of access compared with the law it changes.

  • Because Ordinary bankruptcy already pauses claims against the debtor's assets. The cited lawyers explain that the automatic stay “prevents creditors from enforcing their claims against assets of the bankruptcy estate” [38].
  • Because The same lawyers say the bill “provides an accelerated procedure for stablecoin holders to obtain relief from the automatic stay” [38]. Section 11 requires the issuer's request for release on “the petition date or as soon as practicable thereafter” [3].
  • So The pause is not shown to be a new burden from these rules, and the bill adds a faster release route. This leaves unanswered the PRO's point that wider use would expose more people to any pause that remains.

points.title: The bill expands payments without establishing the refund rights and help users need after theft or mistakes.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill expands payments without establishing the refund rights and help users need after theft or mistakes.

  • Because Established card laws protect against unauthorized transfers: “The Truth-In-Lending Act and the EFTA provide important protection when there are unauthorized transfers.” [39]. EFTA is the federal law governing debit cards and other electronic payments.
  • Because The stablecoin law adds “no protection for unauthorized transfers” [39] and “no error resolution procedure” [39].
  • Because It also omits tools for spotting and resolving missing payments: “Periodic Account Statement Not Required” [39]; “No Customer Service Requirements” [39].
  • Because Users cannot sue just for a breach of the new law's consumer rules: it “does not grant consumers a private right of action” [39].
  • So People who cannot replace stolen or missing payment money need clear refund duties and a way to enforce them. Expanding stablecoin payments without establishing those rights gives [NAME] a reason to protect the people least able to absorb the loss.
points.con_html:
Response Listing protections absent from this bill does not establish that the payment arrangements it would expand lack enforceable rights under other laws.

  • Because Section 6(c) preserves existing rights: “Nothing in this Act may be construed to modify or otherwise affect any right or remedy under any Federal consumer financial law” [3].
  • Because Before July 2025, a federal district court had applied the Electronic Fund Transfer Act to personal cryptocurrency accounts. It held: “Its terms, when properly construed, cover the electronic transfer of funds such as cryptocurrency.” [40]
  • Because The PRO's consumer-law source also recognizes claims under other consumer statutes: “These laws do not preclude consumers from suing in court.” [39] It adds that the bill's preemption section “may preclude consumers from successfully asserting a violation of state law.” [39]
  • So The absence of a new right to sue under S.1582 does not erase payment-law or contract claims, though their reach is unsettled. The PRO needs to establish the claimed refund and help gap under the laws governing the accounts in question; omissions from this one statute do not establish it.

points.title: The bill removes an existing fraud watchdog from permitted stablecoin sales.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 The bill removes an existing fraud watchdog from permitted stablecoin sales.

  • Because The U.S. commodity regulator has used its fraud powers against false stablecoin reserve claims. Its Tether order required “a civil monetary penalty of $41 million” [41] for “making untrue or misleading statements and omissions of material fact” [41].
  • Because Section 17 removes permitted tokens from that regulator's commodity-fraud law: “The term `commodity' does not include a payment stablecoin issued by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer” [3]. A permitted issuer is one approved under the bill.
  • So Removing this route for pursuing dishonest sales takes away a protection already used for stablecoin customers. [NAME]'s concern for protecting weaker customers from powerful firms gives a reason to oppose that loss.
points.con_html:
Response A change of regulator does not establish a loss of protection against the reserve fraud in the Tether example.

  • Because The case concerned claims about backing and outside checks: “Tether misrepresented to customers and the market that Tether maintained sufficient U.S. dollar reserves” [41]; “Tether falsely represented that it would undergo routine, professional audits” [41].
  • Because Section 4 makes full backing a legal duty, “on an at least 1 to 1 basis” [3]. It requires monthly reserve information to be “examined by a registered public accounting firm” [3] and punishes an executive's certification made “knowing that such certification is false” [3].
  • Because Section 6 lets federal supervisors order an issuer to “take affirmative action to correct the conditions resulting from any such violation or practice.” [3] Section 7 gives state supervisors “supervisory, examination, and enforcement authority” [3] over their approved issuers.
  • So The cited misconduct remains subject to direct backing, reporting, and enforcement duties. Counting the lost commodity-law route without assessing these replacements does not show that customers lose protection against that fraud.

points.title: Nationwide approval can take effect without a completed safety decision or another state's licensing check.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Nationwide approval can take effect without a completed safety decision or another state's licensing check.

  • Because A substantially complete federal application must be decided within 120 days. If the regulator misses the deadline, “the application shall be deemed approved.” [3].
  • Because For a federally approved nonbank, that approval would “supersede and preempt any State requirement for a charter, license, or other authorization to do business” [3].
  • So Such an issuer can gain nationwide access through official silence, while states lose the power to require another license before it serves their residents. Protecting residents from entry without a completed safety decision gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this rule.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The 120-day clock starts with a substantially complete application, permitted issuers remain subject to examination, and CRS describes prior state oversight as typically under more limited requirements than the bills proposed. Sources: [3], [18].

points.title: Ordinary holders can face unequal or costly access to their tokens' cash value.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 Ordinary holders can face unequal or costly access to their tokens' cash value.

  • Because The bill requires disclosure of redemption fees but sets “no maximum amount that can be charged.” [39]. Redemption means turning tokens back into money.
  • Because It does not establish equal redemption terms for all customers; Public Citizen identifies room for “favoring some customers over others” [2].
  • Because Access through middlemen is central to the existing business: “most stablecoin users do not transact directly with the issuer” [37]. One documented barrier is Tether's rule that it “imposes a lower bound limit on redemptions of $100,000” [37]. Terms vary by issuer: the same source describes Circle as having “much lower redemption limits and fees.” [37]
  • So Widening use without equal, affordable access to redemption leaves small holders dependent on fees, middlemen, and terms they cannot meet. Fair treatment gives [NAME] a reason to oppose expanding payments on those terms.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.

points.title: The interest ban prevents direct holders from bargaining for a share of their money's earnings.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 The interest ban prevents direct holders from bargaining for a share of their money's earnings.

  • Because The bill bars issuers from paying interest just for holding tokens: “No permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer shall pay the holder of any payment stablecoin any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin.” [3].
  • Because In direct issuer-to-user arrangements, the forgone payments are “instead retained (likely as profit) by the issuer.” [30].
  • So Users supply the money and bear its uninsured risk, yet the law blocks them from bargaining for interest solely for holding it. This preference for firms over their direct customers gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the rule as unfair.
points.con_html:
Response Barring one way to bargain over payment services does not by itself make issuers' reserve income an unjust transfer from their direct customers.

  • Because A payment stablecoin promises a fixed repayment: its issuer “is obligated to convert, redeem, or repurchase for a fixed amount of monetary value” [3]. That promise differs from a share of the issuer's investment earnings.
  • Because Providing that service has costs. The PRO's source explains that issuers face “higher operating costs as they face more stringent capital, liquidity, and risk management standards” [37]. Total income from reserves is therefore not the same as profit taken without providing a service.
  • So The PRO has not explained why funding a payment service from reserve income is unjust unless customers can also bargain for interest. A restriction on that contract term does not by itself establish the unfair preference for firms that the PRO claims.

points.title: Workers owed wages lose priority when legally required reserves are missing.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 Workers owed wages lose priority when legally required reserves are missing.

  • Because For the shortfall in reserves the law required an issuer to maintain, holders' remaining bankruptcy claims “shall have first priority over any other claim, including over any expenses and claims that have priority under that subsection” [3].
  • Because Those displaced claims include “priority wage and tax claims” [38].
  • So When the remaining assets run out, paying token holders first leaves less for workers already owed wages. Protecting those workers and treating their claims justly gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this change.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The super-priority is limited to the shortfall in reserves that Section 4 required the issuer to maintain for holders. Sources: [3].

points.title: Drawing funds away from community banks threatens opportunities in poor and rural communities.
points.pro_html:
Point 9 Drawing funds away from community banks threatens opportunities in poor and rural communities.

  • Because The lending analysis warns that deposits “could flow out of insured depository institutions and into payment stablecoins.” [29].
  • Because Issuers cannot replace those banks' loans directly: “they must invest virtually all their assets in designated short-term financial instruments held as reserves.” [42].
  • Because The resulting lending loss would be “especially acute in rural and low-income areas” [29]; “stablecoins have no community lending obligations.” [29].
  • So Shifting funding away from community banks threatens a source of home, farm, and small-business loans in those places. Protecting people's chances to build a livelihood gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this expansion.
points.con_html:
Response The community-lending forecast relies on a mistaken reading of exposed deposits and skips how reserve purchases affect bank funding.

  • Because Its rural-lending warning rests on “a one-third decline in deposit levels” [29]. Yet CRS describes the underlying transactional-deposit pool as a “$6.6 trillion market” [30] identified as potentially at risk, not a forecast that the whole pool will leave.
  • Because The original Treasury advisory presentation labels its scenarios “Hypothetical Design Components That Could Influence Market Behaviour” [31]. A pool of deposits that could switch is not a predicted outflow.
  • Because Buying Treasury backing can return the money to banks through the seller. In that case, the Council of Economic Advisers explains that total deposits are “unchanged—they have simply moved from one institution to another.” [32]
  • So Stablecoin balances do not measure deposits lost to the banking system. A claim about poor and rural borrowers also needs to establish which local banks lose usable funding. The cited forecast does not supply that link merely because issuers cannot make loans themselves.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The PPI lending warning builds on a $6.6 trillion figure that CRS and the Treasury advisory presentation describe as at risk or hypothetical. CEA's April 2026 baseline estimates that eliminating stablecoin yield would raise bank lending by $2.1 billion (0.02%), with $500 million from community banks (0.026%). Sources: [30], [31], [32].

points.title: A run can carry private payment risks into the wider economy and public finances.
points.pro_html:
Point 10 A run can carry private payment risks into the wider economy and public finances.

  • Because The bill permits bank deposits as backing. A rush to cash out tokens can therefore pull funds from banks: “a stablecoin issuer deemed at risk of breaking the buck could lead to a rapid withdrawal of deposits at banks that otherwise were sound.” [37]. Breaking the buck means falling below the promised dollar value.
  • Because Forced sales of backing assets can spread the stress: “These dynamics could create fire-sale patterns and turn a stablecoin run into stress on the banking system.” [43]. A fire sale is a hurried sale to raise cash.
  • Because A major issuer's collapse “could affect pensions, savings, small business loans, and more.” [6].
  • Because Pressure for a public rescue follows the same crisis: “Regulators would feel compelled to step in to prevent the collapse of the payment system.” [44]. If taxpayers fund a rescue, “even those who never engaged with crypto could bear the cost.” [6].
  • So Expanding these links exposes uninvolved workers, retirees, borrowers, and taxpayers to private firms' risks. [NAME] has reason to protect vulnerable people from the spillover and resist making strangers pay for it.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Section 4 requires capital, liquidity and diversification rules still to be written, and it conditions repo use. Brookings frames the fire-sale danger as arising without appropriate standards; CSIS says the Act imposes no hard liquidity, concentration or stress-testing requirements. Sources: [3], [13], [43].

points.title: Commercial platforms gain another way to pressure people who depend on them for income.
points.pro_html:
Point 11 Commercial platforms gain another way to pressure people who depend on them for income.

  • Because The bill does not bar commercial issuers whose shares are not publicly traded: “privately held nonfinancial companies are not prohibited from issuing stablecoins.” [13]. The bill does not create the combination of commerce and payments, but by removing regulatory uncertainty it makes this route more usable.
  • Because A platform can use its existing business to “raise the costs of switching to other payment products” [13]. Public Citizen gives the example of a retailer that “might disfavor a subcontractor if it failed to use the aggregator's stablecoin.” [2].
  • Because The bill's rule against forcing customers to buy another product may not reach this pressure from an issuer's affiliate. It is “significantly narrower than the statutory prohibition on tying applicable to banks, which applies to both the bank and its affiliates.” [45]
  • So Expanding this business model exposes small sellers and workers to payment terms they cannot readily refuse without risking income. Equal opportunity gives [NAME] a reason to resist making this power easier to use.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: CRS says firms are generally allowed to blend commercial and financial activities outside banking. Public commercial companies need a unanimous committee finding covering safety, data limits and tying compliance; privately held firms are not subject to that committee route. Sources: [18], [3].

points.title: Commercial issuance gives firms more payment data for steering customers' choices and prices.
points.pro_html:
Point 12 Commercial issuance gives firms more payment data for steering customers' choices and prices.

  • Because Combining commerce with stablecoin issuance gives firms access to “detailed information about their financial assets and spending patterns.” [42].
  • Because The bill's special limits on advertising, sale, and sharing of payment data by covered public companies have an exception: “unless the public company receives consent from the consumer” [3].
  • Because This data has practical uses beyond advertising. The FTC found that pricing firms “can show higher priced products based on consumers’ search and purchase activity.” [46].
  • So Giving sellers more financial information gives them another tool for steering people toward more expensive choices based on their needs. Protecting customers from that unequal power gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the expansion.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: CRS says firms are generally allowed to blend commercial and financial activities outside banking. Public commercial companies need a unanimous committee finding covering safety, data limits and tying compliance; privately held firms are not subject to that committee route. Sources: [18], [3].

points.title: Expanding the President's stablecoin business increases the risk of privileged access to public power.
points.pro_html:
Point 13 Expanding the President's stablecoin business increases the risk of privileged access to public power.

  • Because The Trump family's stablecoin business stands to benefit from wider use, while the bill's stated ethics safeguard “wouldn’t apply to the President or Vice-President” [36].
  • Because Critics quoted by The New Yorker say that a Trump-owned stablecoin “creates new possibilities for interested parties to funnel money to him and his companies.” [36].
  • So Enlarging a business through which interested parties can enrich the President gives wealthy interests another route to seek favor. Just treatment of everyone, including people without that financial access, gives [NAME] a reason to oppose expanding this channel.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: USD1 existed before the vote, with a reported market cap of about $2.2 billion in June 2025. Section 4 preserves existing ethics statutes. Sources: [36], [3].

points.title: Wider dollar-token use threatens financial stability in vulnerable foreign economies.
points.pro_html:
Point 14 Wider dollar-token use threatens financial stability in vulnerable foreign economies.

  • Because Making dollar stablecoins more attractive can cause “greater substitution away from local foreign currencies.” [37].
  • Because This makes money easier to move out quickly: “users can hold dollar proxies at home that can be instantly exchanged for real dollars offshore.” [7]. The risk is greater in “already volatile markets facing high inflation and sharp currency swings.” [7].
  • Because Wider substitution can also “undermine the monetary policy sovereignty of foreign countries.” [37]—their ability to manage their own money and economic conditions.
  • So Promoting dollar tokens exposes people in weaker economies to faster financial outflows and weaker tools for stabilizing their economies. [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people everywhere gives a reason to oppose imposing those risks on strangers abroad.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Brookings notes that countries may ban or limit USD stablecoins domestically, and lists cash, demand deposits and money market funds as forms of payments media that may shrink. Sources: [37].

points.title: Replacing public cash shifts income away from shared public needs.
points.pro_html:
Point 15 Replacing public cash shifts income away from shared public needs.

  • Because When stablecoins replace currency, the income from issuing money changes hands: “the seigniorage of stablecoins would accrue to the stablecoin issuer rather than the U.S. Treasury.” [37]. Seigniorage means income earned from issuing money.
  • Because Foreign governments can also lose this income; “for countries struggling with low tax-to-GDP revenue, this could represent a significant loss.” [7]. These are countries already collecting little tax relative to their economies.
  • So Even without a financial crisis, this shift reduces public income available for shared services and opportunities. Taking resources from governments already short of funds gives [NAME] a reason to protect the people who depend on those resources.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Brookings notes that countries may ban or limit USD stablecoins domestically, and lists cash, demand deposits and money market funds as forms of payments media that may shrink. Sources: [37].

points.title: The public helps pay to oversee firms' new payment business.
points.pro_html:
Point 16 The public helps pay to oversee firms' new payment business.

  • Because The bill creates new costs for the Federal Reserve to oversee stablecoins. CBO explains who bears them: “Costs incurred by the Federal Reserve reduce remittances to the Treasury” [47]. Remittances are the income the Fed sends to the government.
  • Because CBO estimates that these administrative costs would reduce federal “revenues by $73 million over the 2025-2035 period.” [47].
  • So The public supplies part of the cost of running this private payment system, including people who never use it. Fair treatment gives [NAME] a reason to oppose placing those costs on the public instead of the firms earning the income.
points.con_html:
Response Public payment for oversight is not, by itself, an unfair subsidy for firms' payment operations.

  • Because CBO says the expense funds “examinations, risk monitoring, enforcement, and certifying state regulators.” [47] It estimates a reduction in “revenues by $73 million over the 2025-2035 period.” [47] This estimate measures the public cost of supervision over eleven fiscal years.
  • Because Section 6 directs examinations at risks to “the stability of the financial system of the United States” [3]. The spending therefore buys protection for people outside the issuer-customer relationship.
  • So Nonusers help fund oversight from which nonusers also benefit. The PRO supplies no reason why sharing the cost of this public protection treats them unjustly; the fact that firms could instead be charged does not establish that conclusion.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: CBO reports OCC and NCUA collect fees offsetting part of their costs, for net direct spending of $47 million versus $77 million gross, and that Federal Reserve remittances have largely been suspended, which affects the timing of the $73 million revenue effect. Sources: [47].
