pages.description: S.1582 creates federal rules for "stablecoins" — digital coins an issuer must redeem for a fixed dollar value. Only permitted, regulated companies may issue them, and each coin must be fully backed one-to-one by cash or similar safe assets that issuers may not lend out.
pages.comparison: If this bill took effect on July 17, 2025, versus law in force then

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.1582?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect S.1582 would create national licensing and safeguards for payment stablecoins, “digital assets which an issuer must redeem for a fixed value” [1]. On July 17, 2025, they were regulated “as money transmitters, primarily at the state level” [2]. The bill would require permitted issuers to back their tokens with reserves “on an at least 1 to 1 basis” [3]. If an issuer fails, holders would get priority on those reserves: “over the claims of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and any other holder of claims against the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, with respect to required payment stablecoin reserves” [3].

points.title: The licensing system would require officials to hear applicants who challenge their decisions.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 The licensing system would require officials to hear applicants who challenge their decisions.

  • Because Different kinds of provider could qualify: “Stablecoins could be issued by banks and credit unions (through subsidiaries) or nonbanks.” [4]
  • Because Federal regulators could reject a substantially complete application only on safety grounds: “the activities of the applicant would be unsafe or unsound based on the factors described in subsection (c)” [3].
  • Because Applicants who appeal in time would have a right to present their case: “the applicant may appear, personally or through counsel, to submit written materials or provide oral testimony and oral argument” [3].
  • Because Listening to people who contest a decision puts tolerance into practice: disagreement does not erase their chance to explain themselves.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to support a system that judges applicants by safety and hears their reasons when they disagree with a refusal.
points.con_html:
Response Hearing a dispute about an issuer's fitness does not show listening to people across the differences named by this value.

  • Because Section 5 ties refusal to whether “the activities of the applicant would be unsafe or unsound based on the factors described in subsection (c)” [3]. Those factors include “financial condition and resources” [3] and “The competence, experience, and integrity of the officers, directors, and principal shareholders” [3].
  • Because The hearing is “to appeal the denial” [3]. It lets the applicant present evidence and arguments about that decision: “the applicant may appear, personally or through counsel, to submit written materials or provide oral testimony and oral argument” [3].
  • Because The range of eligible applicants concerns business forms: “Stablecoins could be issued by banks and credit unions (through subsidiaries) or nonbanks.” [4] That range, and a dispute over meeting safety rules, do not show differences in the people involved, their backgrounds, or their beliefs.
  • So The PRO shows a way to challenge a licensing decision. It does not show that this process puts listening to and accepting different people into practice. Disagreement about an application cannot supply that missing link by itself.

points.title: The bill would add protection to a payment route outside the companies and banks that can shut out unpopular voices.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill would add protection to a payment route outside the companies and banks that can shut out unpopular voices.

  • Because EFF reports a lawsuit alleging “targeting payments associated with Islam or Arab nationalities or ethnicity” [5] and “numerous examples of sex worker advocates facing account closures” [5].
  • Because Stablecoins can move on networks open to users without a payment company's approval to join. CRS describes these networks as “decentralized, public, permissionless” [6].
  • Because Federal regulators could not reject an issuer simply for using such a network: “The issuance of a payment stablecoin on an open, public, or decentralized network shall not be a valid ground for denial of an application received under subsection (a).” [3]
  • Because Section 3's new issuance and sales limits exempt “the direct transfer of digital assets between 2 individuals acting on their own behalf and for their own lawful purposes, without the involvement of an intermediary” [3].
  • Because Section 3 also exempts payments through wallets people control themselves: “any transaction by means of a software or hardware wallet that facilitates an individual's own custody of digital assets” [3].
  • Because This route has served people outside an authoritarian state's banks. Circle's USDC aid to Venezuelan health workers was designed “to bypass the controls imposed by Maduro over the domestic financial system” [7].
  • Because Circle cites Amnesty International's reports of “healthcare workers being arrested for speaking out about unsafe working practices since the pandemic began” [7].
  • So The bill would add reserve and bankruptcy rights to regulated tokens while preserving open networks, lawful direct payments and wallets people control themselves. That protects funds sent through an alternative to ordinary payment gatekeepers.
  • Because Accepting people despite disagreement gives [NAME] a reason to protect the means they use to speak, organize and support one another.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to favor protections for a payment route that supports lawful voices and ties beyond the approval of ordinary payment companies or authoritarian banks.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not show why protecting funds on an alternative payment route amounts to support for accepting unpopular voices.

  • Because Section 11 concerns “any insolvency proceeding of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer under Federal or State law” [3]. Its repayment priority applies “with respect to required payment stablecoin reserves” [3]. This addresses an issuer's failure to repay, a different risk from refusing a user's lawful speech or group ties.
  • Because The direct-transfer and personal-wallet exceptions begin “This section shall not apply to” [3]. They limit section 3's new restrictions. The open-network rule likewise bars a particular reason for refusing an issuer's application: “The issuance of a payment stablecoin on an open, public, or decentralized network shall not be a valid ground for denial of an application received under subsection (a).” [3]
  • Because The EFF report cites allegations of “targeting payments associated with Islam or Arab nationalities or ethnicity” [5] and reports “numerous examples of sex worker advocates facing account closures” [5]. These passages describe the refusals that motivate the PRO's tolerance claim.
  • Because The Venezuelan source identifies a financial barrier: “typical bank receipts are subject to rigged forex rates” [7]. It also reports “healthcare workers being arrested for speaking out about unsafe working practices since the pandemic began” [7]. It does not identify those arrested workers as aid recipients or show that recipients had been refused payments for their views.
  • Because Accepting people despite disagreement does not mean favoring every safeguard for a tool they could use. The PRO needs to connect this protection of money to supporting people across their differences.
  • So The examples describe payment exclusion and a way to deliver aid beyond currency controls. They do not show that the new financial protection supports the speaking, organizing, or acceptance of unpopular voices. Reports of arrests among healthcare workers cannot establish that claim for the aid recipients.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Permitted issuers must be able to comply with lawful orders; Steptoe says freezing can reach tokens in non-custodial wallets, and issuers will likely need some centralized control such as blacklisting. Sources: [8].

points.title: The bill would protect payment choices that fit migrants' and displaced people's different lives.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill would protect payment choices that fit migrants' and displaced people's different lives.

  • Because International money transfers “matter greatly for immigrant communities sending money to families abroad” [9].
  • Because MoneyGram's 2022 service used “Circle's USD Coin (USDC)” [10] and let wallet users move between cash and digital currency “all without requiring a bank account or credit card” [10].
  • Because UNHCR's USDC aid pilot put funds in phone wallets, “allowing people to travel within the country or cross borders without the need to carry cash” [11].
  • Because UNHCR explains why different payment options matter: “It’s also essential to provide people with a range of options for receiving aid, as one size does not fit all.” [11]
  • Because The bill would require issuers to “disclose in plain language all fees associated with purchasing or redeeming the payment stablecoins” [3].
  • Because Users would get advance warning of issuer fee changes: “such fees can only be changed upon not less than 7 days' prior notice to consumers” [3].
  • So Reserve and bankruptcy rights would protect regulated tokens used in these payments, while clear issuer fees would help users choose how to pay. These protections support ways of helping relatives and receiving aid that fit life across borders or without a bank account.
  • Because Accepting people whose lives differ includes making room for their cross-border family ties and their own choices about receiving help.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to favor protections that accommodate those choices and circumstances.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO treats protecting people's money and payment choices as accepting different people without defending that step.

  • Because The aid pilot serves practical needs: UNHCR says the funds help people “cover basic needs like rent of accommodation, food, medical care and heating during the winter” [11]. MoneyGram describes access “all without requiring a bank account or credit card” [10]. These passages show why the payment tools are useful.
  • Because The bill's fee rule requires issuers to “disclose in plain language all fees associated with purchasing or redeeming the payment stablecoins” [3], with changes allowed only “upon not less than 7 days' prior notice to consumers” [3]. Those are information rights about buying and redeeming tokens.
  • Because The bankruptcy rule protects “the claim of a person holding payment stablecoins issued by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer” [3]. The basis for this right is holding the token, whatever the holder's background or payment purpose.
  • Because Accepting people across differences is distinct from making any useful service safer for them. Identifying migrants or displaced people as users does not make every financial benefit to those users an expression of tolerance.
  • So The PRO connects the bill to protection of money and information about issuer fees. It leaves the next step unsupported: why those changes express acceptance of cross-border family ties or different lives. The examples' usefulness does not show that value connection.

points.title: The bill would give users control over commercial uses of payment data that reveal their beliefs and group ties.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 The bill would give users control over commercial uses of payment data that reveal their beliefs and group ties.

  • Because Linking identities to stablecoin payments can reveal “donations, memberships, habits, beliefs, and associations” [12].
  • Because Data brokers sort people by sensitive differences, including “their ethnicity or religion, their political affiliation, or their expected levels of spending” [13].
  • Because The Brennan Center identifies risks of “discrimination in housing, employment, and credit decisions” [13] from this commercial data market.
  • Because For covered public companies mainly outside finance, section 4(a)(12) restricts commercial uses of private personal information from stablecoin transactions “unless the public company receives consent from the consumer” [3].
  • Because Uses requiring consent include “used to target, personalize, or rank advertising or other content” [3], “sold to any third party” [3] and “shared with non- affiliates” [3].
  • So Users could refuse these covered issuers permission to turn their private payment records into advertising profiles or pass them to commercial outsiders. This restricts a route through which beliefs and group ties become information used to sort and exclude people.
  • Because Tolerance gives [NAME] a reason to protect people's ability to keep different beliefs and associations without those differences becoming grounds for unfair treatment.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to favor these limits on commercial exposure of people's differences.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Brennan Center describes brokers drawing on many sources, including public records, app developers, ISPs and others, and does not mention stablecoin data. The consent condition covers targeting, personalizing or ranking advertising or other content, sale and sharing with non-affiliates; it does not list a covered firm's own decisions about whom to serve, sharing within its corporate group, or government access. Coin Center's stated threats include government surveillance. Sources: [13], [3], [12].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose S.1582?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect The bill makes permission to issue payment stablecoins—“digital assets which an issuer must redeem for a fixed value” [1]—depend on government approval and financial-crime controls. Section 3(a) says: “It shall be unlawful for any person other than a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to issue a payment stablecoin in the United States.” [3] Section 4 makes payment-blocking powers a condition of permission: “A permitted payment stablecoin issuer may issue payment stablecoins only if the issuer has the technological capability to comply, and will comply, with the terms of any lawful order.” [3]

points.title: More detailed customer checks increase the risk of rejecting religious and ethnic communities as suspect groups.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 More detailed customer checks increase the risk of rejecting religious and ethnic communities as suspect groups.

  • Because Section 4(a)(5)(v) requires “appropriate enhanced due diligence” [3], meaning closer customer checks. Steptoe identifies a change for some issuers in these checks, known as KYC: “Therefore, these more granular KYC obligations will be an important change for some issuers.” [8]
  • Because Checking customers can make their accounts unprofitable. Treasury's bank interviews found that checking nonprofit accounts “requires many resources and is often not profitable.” [14] Its nonprofit consultations found that “diligence sometimes leads to closing accounts.” [14]
  • Because Avoiding penalties adds another incentive to reject customers. A 2024 congressional letter explains: “Banks are incentivized to close accounts in order to avoid enforcement” [15].
  • Because The same letter identifies who is exposed to this practice: “Financial institutions may consider Muslim and Arab, Middle Eastern, and South Asian Americans “high risk,” potentially erroneously, when sending payments or remittances abroad or donating to charities or religious institutions.” [15]
  • So Adding more detailed checks to stablecoin issuance strengthens a known incentive to reject customers whose ordinary religious giving or family payments abroad appear risky.
  • Because Accepting people across religious and cultural differences gives [NAME] a reason to resist treating those differences as grounds for blanket rejection.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to oppose extending this risk of group-based exclusion to more stablecoin issuers and their customers.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: FinCEN's 2019 guidance required MSB AML programs including verifying customer identification and risk-based controls. A bank-agency statement says there is no requirement for unique additional diligence for charities or nonprofits as a class. S.1582 directs tailored rules, and bank CIP rules allow non-documentary procedures. Sources: [16], [17], [18], [3].

points.title: Added identity checks raise the risk of excluding people whose documents or life histories do not fit an issuer's usual process.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Added identity checks raise the risk of excluding people whose documents or life histories do not fit an issuer's usual process.

  • Because Section 4(a)(5)(v) requires “identification and verification of account holders with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer” [3]. This adds formal rules for some issuers operating as money-transfer firms. Steptoe explains their current freedom over customer checks: “MSBs are not subject to CIP or CDD rules, meaning they have additional flexibility with respect to how they KYC users.” [8] MSBs are money-services businesses, including money-transfer firms. CIP, CDD and KYC refer to identity and customer-risk checks.
  • Because Treasury's January 2025 working draft, based on stakeholder roundtables, calls lack of suitable identification “a primary barrier many communities face in accessing the financial system.” [19]
  • Because The draft records different sources of that barrier: “Refugees and asylees may arrive in the United States without adequate identification documents.” [19] It also reports that “Tribal IDs used by Indigenous communities may not be recognized by financial institutions as a valid form of identification.” [19]
  • Because Name and gender changes create another mismatch: “Transgender and nonbinary people face a patchwork of state policies that make it challenging to update gender markers on IDs or to make legal name changes.” [19] People leaving prison also reported “loss or confiscation of identification documents during incarceration.” [19]
  • Because Outcomes depend on how the rules and issuers handle these cases. The same draft describes institutions that “use alternative IDs or non-documentary verification methods” [19], and Steptoe says “It remains to be seen whether PPSIs will be subject to CIP/CDD requirements that match existing rules for other BSA-regulated financial institutions” [8].
  • So The bill extends more detailed verification duties to issuers serving people whom existing financial checks already struggle to recognize. Where issuers do not adopt such alternatives, that raises the risk of rejection from direct accounts for people with these backgrounds and identities.
  • Because Accepting people across different backgrounds and identities gives [NAME] a reason to resist excluding them when their documents differ or are hard to replace.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to oppose extending this barrier to participation.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: FinCEN's 2019 guidance required MSB AML programs including verifying customer identification and risk-based controls. A bank-agency statement says there is no requirement for unique additional diligence for charities or nonprofits as a class. S.1582 directs tailored rules, and bank CIP rules allow non-documentary procedures. Sources: [16], [17], [18], [3].

points.title: Wider monitoring puts private ties to unpopular groups at greater risk of exposure, deterring participation.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Wider monitoring puts private ties to unpopular groups at greater risk of exposure, deterring participation.

  • Because Section 9(d) requires new guidance and rules covering “Standards for payment stablecoin issuers' systems and practices to monitor transactions on blockchains” [3]. Blockchains are shared digital records of transfers.
  • Because This opens a wider field for monitoring than issuers' current duties. Steptoe explains: “At present, stablecoin issuers are responsible for AML compliance with respect to primary market transactions to which they are a party, but are not expected to monitor all transactions across the entirety of the blockchain.” [8] Here, AML means checks against money laundering, and primary transactions are purchases or sales involving the issuer itself.
  • Because The final reach depends on rulemaking. Steptoe reads the text as one that “strongly suggests that FinCEN's rules or guidance will expect PPSIs to monitor and intervene in transactions in both the primary and, to at least some degree, secondary markets.” [8]
  • Because Tracking can reach transfers between people who hold their own tokens: “stablecoins can be tracked across a blockchain as they move between holders, even when the transfers happen between wallets that are unhosted by intermediaries.” [20]
  • So Combining identified issuer accounts with wider tracing makes donations, dues and other payments easier to link to people beyond their dealings with the issuer. To the extent the rules require that monitoring, the bill creates an added route for exposing their group ties.
  • Because Exposure of such ties can deter association. In NAACP v. Alabama, the Supreme Court recorded that exposure of members' identities had brought “economic reprisal, loss of employment, threat of physical coercion, and other manifestations of public hostility.” [21]
  • Because Government collection itself adds risk. In its 2021 decision on donor records, Americans for Prosperity Foundation v. Bonta, the Court said deterrence can occur even with “no disclosure to the general public.” [22] It explained that “each governmental demand for disclosure brings with it an additional risk of chill.” [22]
  • Because [NAME]'s wish to listen to and understand different people gives [NAME] a reason to protect the private support and contact that let unpopular groups speak and be heard.
  • So By opening more transfers to monitoring, the bill increases the risk of deterring the support and contact that let different groups be heard and understood. That gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
points.con_html:
Response FinCEN's later proposal does not support the added monitoring on which this reason depends.

  • Because In April 2026, FinCEN proposed rules for issuers and stated: “FinCEN is not proposing to require a PPSI as part of an AML/CFT program to monitor secondary market activity” [23]. It also stated: “FinCEN is also not proposing to require PPSIs to file SARs on secondary market transactions” [23]. Secondary-market activity is activity not directly involving the issuer.
  • Because Section 9's separate rules must be “based on the results of the research and risk assessments required under this section” [3]. That research must consider “Privacy risks associated with the information that is collected or reviewed.” [3]
  • So The proposal is not final and Section 9's standards remain to be written, so the outcome is open. On this record, the PRO's step from the bill to issuers monitoring transfers beyond their own dealings is unsupported. The disclosure cases explain why exposure matters, but cannot establish that the bill increases it.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Tether announced Chainalysis monitoring of secondary markets in 2024 and confirmed adoption in May 2025. Section 9 research must consider the amount and sensitivity of information and privacy risks, and FinCEN's guidance or rules are due within 3 years. The cited Cato commentary discusses earlier bill drafts. The two Supreme Court cases concern government demands for membership or donor records. Sources: [24], [25], [3], [20].

Evidence note: FinCEN and OFAC's April 2026 proposed rule would apply secondary-market obligations to blocking, freezing and rejecting impermissible transactions and to complying with lawful orders. It does not propose requiring issuers, as part of an AML/CFT program, to monitor secondary-market activity or file SARs on secondary-market transactions, and it requests comment. Section 9(d) rulemaking is separate. Sources: [23].

points.title: Mandatory payment-blocking powers strengthen financial exclusion over disputed international judicial work.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Mandatory payment-blocking powers strengthen financial exclusion over disputed international judicial work.

  • Because The bill's freezing requirement adds a legal condition, including for issuers that did not build this power into their tokens. Steptoe explains: “However, the GENIUS Act now makes such capabilities a legal prerequisite for operation.” [8]
  • Because Foreign issuers also need this capability to reach U.S. customers through digital-asset services: “unless the foreign payment stablecoin issuer has the technological capability to comply, and will comply, with the terms of any lawful order and any reciprocal arrangement pursuant to section 18.” [3]
  • Because Existing sanctions already targeted International Criminal Court judges over their rulings. UN News reported the UN rights chief's criticism that the sanctions “attack the judges for performing their judicial functions” [26].
  • Because The February 2025 sanctions order expressly covers foreign people found “to have directly engaged in any effort by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute a protected person without consent of that person’s country of nationality” [27]. Covered assets “are blocked and may not be transferred, paid, exported, withdrawn, or otherwise dealt in” [27].
  • Because Section 4(a)(6)(A) directs Treasury to coordinate with issuers so they can “effectively block a payment stablecoin of the foreign person” [3] when it acts to block that person's property.
  • So Requiring issuers to build and use freezing powers strengthens the means to enforce existing financial penalties against people for judicial work the U.S. government rejects.
  • Note Requiring a lawful order does not resolve that conflict with tolerance. Section 4(a)(5)(vi) also requires “maintenance of an effective economic sanctions compliance program, including verification of sanctions lists, consistent with Federal law.” [3] The existing order makes the judicial work it specifies a ground for sanctions. Stronger enforcement of those penalties is the harm to acceptance at issue.
  • Note Holding tokens in one's own wallet does not remove issuer control. Steptoe explains that freezing reaches tokens “held by persons with no relationship to the issuer and regardless of whether the tokens are in a custodial or non-custodial wallet.” [8]
  • Because Accepting people despite disagreement gives [NAME] a reason to resist cutting them off from ordinary payments over disputed legal judgments, across national and political differences.
  • So [NAME] has a reason to oppose making that financial exclusion easier to enforce.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not explain why accepting people despite disagreement gives [NAME] a reason to resist penalties for the judges' exercise of court power.

  • Because The sanctions order targets efforts to “investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute a protected person without consent of that person’s country of nationality” [27]. The cited dispute therefore concerns the exercise of court power over others, not simply the expression of a different view.
  • Because Section 4 allows an issuer to issue stablecoins only if it “has the technological capability to comply, and will comply, with the terms of any lawful order.” [3] This adds a means of enforcing sanctions; it supplies no premise about why this particular use conflicts with tolerance.
  • Because Tolerance supports accepting people and hearing their views. The PRO needs an added premise that cutting off ordinary payments for this exercise of court power rejects the judges for their differences. Describing the judicial work as disputed does not establish that premise.
  • So The example moves from a disagreement about court power to a claim about rejecting different people without supporting that move. Making the sanctions easier to enforce cannot fill this gap. Calling them lawful cannot fill it either.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Permitted issuers must be able to comply with lawful orders; Steptoe says freezing can reach tokens in non-custodial wallets, and issuers will likely need some centralized control such as blacklisting. Sources: [8].

pages.description: S.1582 creates federal rules for "stablecoins" — digital coins an issuer must redeem for a fixed dollar value. Only permitted, regulated companies may issue them, and each coin must be fully backed one-to-one by cash or similar safe assets that issuers may not lend out.
pages.comparison: If this bill took effect on July 17, 2025, versus law in force then

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.1582?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect S.1582 would strengthen controls on payment stablecoins, digital payment tokens “redeemable at a predetermined fixed amount (e.g., $1).” [1] It builds on existing law: “reporting requirements for anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) apply equally to the transmission of crypto assets.” [2] Section 4 makes the ability and duty to obey federal blocking orders a condition of issuing tokens: “only if the issuer has the technological capability to comply, and will comply, with the terms of any lawful order.” [3] These orders can require issuers to “seize, freeze, burn, or prevent the transfer of payment stablecoins issued by the person” [3]. Section 8 also conditions foreign stablecoins’ availability through U.S. service providers on the issuer’s ability to obey and actual compliance. Treasury can enforce this through a notice “prohibiting digital asset service providers from facilitating secondary trading of payment stablecoins issued by the foreign payment stablecoin issuer in the United States.” [3]

points.title: Disrupting payments for fentanyl ingredients helps prevent fatal poisoning.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Disrupting payments for fentanyl ingredients helps prevent fatal poisoning.

  • Because Drug traffickers use stablecoins to buy ingredients and equipment: “Mexico-based TCOs are increasingly purchasing fentanyl precursor chemicals and manufacturing equipment from PRC-based suppliers in virtual currency, including bitcoin, ether, monero, and tether, among others.” [4]
  • Because The bill requires “monitoring and reporting of any suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation” [3].
  • Because It also adds yearly declarations that issuers have put crime-control programs in place: “on an annual basis thereafter” and “a certification that the issuer has implemented anti-money laundering and economic sanctions compliance programs” [3].
  • Because Such reporting helps investigators stop the suppliers: it lets them “follow the money behind the illicit fentanyl supply chain, identify and prosecute the illicit actors” [4].
  • Because The danger reaches Americans seeking medicine. The Drug Enforcement Administration reports fake pills sold to “unsuspecting customers in the United States who believe they are purchasing real pharmaceutical drugs” [5].
  • Because These pills can cause fatal poisoning. Treasury’s financial crime agency, FinCEN, reports deaths where “victims were unaware that other illicit drugs or counterfeit prescription medications they used contained lethal doses of fentanyl.” [4]
  • So Required reporting, yearly accountability, and enforceable blocking duties strengthen investigators’ means to interrupt ingredient purchases and the production they support. Cutting this supply of poisonous drugs serves [NAME]’s interest in protecting health and avoiding danger.
points.con_html:
Response The fentanyl evidence does not connect the added issuer oversight to newly detected ingredient purchases.

  • Because Suppliers hide purchases behind front companies to “create the façade of a legitimate transaction and to obfuscate the source of the illicit diversion.” [4]
  • Because The yearly statement confirms a crime-control program: “a certification that the issuer has implemented anti-money laundering and economic sanctions compliance programs” [3]. It supplies no information about a particular buyer or purchase.
  • Because An issuer can see a transfer yet lack the facts needed to recognize a crime. FinCEN explains that an issuer can use tracing tools yet “may have limited distinct insight particularly as to the parties associated with, or the purpose of, the transfer.” [6] In the same April 2026 proposal, “FinCEN is also not proposing to require PPSIs to file SARs on secondary market transactions” [6]. Secondary-market transactions are those not directly involving the issuer.
  • So This leaves blocking of purchases once identified unanswered. The missing step is identifying concealed purchases: the PRO has not shown how reporting and yearly accountability supply that information.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: FinCEN and OFAC's April 2026 proposed rule would apply secondary-market obligations to blocking, freezing and rejecting impermissible transactions and to complying with lawful orders. It does not propose requiring issuers, as part of an AML/CFT program, to monitor secondary-market activity or file SARs on secondary-market transactions, and it requests comment. Section 9(d) rulemaking is separate. Sources: [6].

Evidence note: Before the comparison date, stablecoin administrators were to register as MSBs with reporting duties. Tether had a secondary-market sanctions policy from December 2023 and assisted in the March 2025 Garantex and Hamas actions, the 2023 scam seizure and the freeze of a Huione Pay account in July 2024. The FBI's Level Up program contacts victims directly. Sources: [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13].

points.title: Disrupting ransomware profits helps protect hospital care and emergency help.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Disrupting ransomware profits helps protect hospital care and emergency help.

  • Because Ransomware attacks lock computer systems or threaten to expose data to demand payment. They can cause “disrupted emergency services” and “hospital delays” [14].
  • Because Garantex hid ransomware profits. It was sanctioned “for its role in facilitating money laundering of funds from ransomware actors and darknet markets.” [9]
  • Because An actual freeze shows that stablecoins on this route can be blocked: “Stablecoin issuer Tether has frozen $28 million worth of USDT on Russian crypto exchange Garantex.” [15]
  • Because These services help sustain attacks. Treasury states: “Virtual currency exchanges such as SUEX are critical to the profitability of ransomware attacks, which help fund additional cybercriminal activity.” [16]
  • Because Section 9 requires FinCEN to write tracing standards, including “Standards for payment stablecoin issuers' systems and practices to monitor transactions on blockchains, digital asset mixing services, tumblers” [3]. These last two kinds of services hide payment trails.
  • So Required tracing standards and enforceable freezes strengthen the means to find and deny ransomware profits. Attacking this source of funding and profit helps protect the medical care and emergency response [NAME] relies on.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO's tracing standards do not establish added detection of ransomware profits.

  • Because Section 9 requires future guidance and rules “based on the results of the research and risk assessments required under this section” [3]. It directs the development of tracing standards; it does not specify a new way to identify targets that “moved its operational cryptocurrency wallets to different virtual currency addresses on a daily basis” [9].
  • Because FinCEN's April 2026 proposal for issuers' crime-control programs, which is separate from Section 9, states: “FinCEN is not proposing to require a PPSI as part of an AML/CFT program to monitor secondary market activity” [6].
  • So This leaves enforceable freezes of identified funds unanswered. It challenges only the step from required tracing standards to finding more ransomware profits, which remains unsettled while those rules are unwritten.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: FinCEN and OFAC's April 2026 proposed rule would apply secondary-market obligations to blocking, freezing and rejecting impermissible transactions and to complying with lawful orders. It does not propose requiring issuers, as part of an AML/CFT program, to monitor secondary-market activity or file SARs on secondary-market transactions, and it requests comment. Section 9(d) rulemaking is separate. Sources: [6].

Evidence note: Before the comparison date, stablecoin administrators were to register as MSBs with reporting duties. Tether had a secondary-market sanctions policy from December 2023 and assisted in the March 2025 Garantex and Hamas actions, the 2023 scam seizure and the freeze of a Huione Pay account in July 2024. The FBI's Level Up program contacts victims directly. Sources: [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13].

points.title: Blocking terrorist funds helps protect people in the United States from violence.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Blocking terrorist funds helps protect people in the United States from violence.

  • Because ISIS uses “stablecoins like Tether (USDT) to raise and move funds” [17].
  • Because Its money supports both violence and its promotion. The coalition against ISIS financing seeks to deprive it of “resources to commit atrocities and spread its extremist ideology.” [18]
  • Because This promotion threatens people at home. FinCEN reports that ISIS urges “attacks in the United States and Western countries” [17].
  • Because This route runs through ISIS's wider funding and promotion, not through direct payment for most attacks at home. The same advisory says “HVE activities tend to be funded through legal means, like personal savings and the sale of personal assets.” [17] HVE means homegrown violent extremist.
  • Because Seizing stablecoins has already disrupted terrorist financing. In a case involving USDT intended for Hamas, the FBI reported: “By successfully disrupting access to these funds, we have weakened their ability to function,” [10].
  • Because The bill makes foreign issuers’ access through U.S. providers depend on blocking capability and compliance: “unless the foreign payment stablecoin issuer has the technological capability to comply and complies with the terms of any lawful order.” [3]
  • So The bill adds pressure to carry out freezes against terrorist funds. Denying these resources restricts support for violence and the promotion of attacks on Americans. That advances [NAME]’s personal safety at home.
points.con_html:
Response The terrorism evidence does not show that added U.S. trading pressure would cut funding for U.S. attacks or the propaganda that encourages them.

  • Because For the costs of domestic attacks, the PRO's ISIS source says homegrown violent extremists' activities tend to be “funded through legal means, like personal savings” [17]. That evidence does not connect their attack budgets to the overseas stablecoin fundraising cited.
  • Because For propaganda, the coalition states its aim of denying ISIS “resources to commit atrocities and spread its extremist ideology.” [18] This goal supplies no evidence that an issuer's failure to obey a freezing order sustains that propaganda.
  • So This leaves the added pressure to freeze terrorist funds unanswered. It challenges the further step to personal safety in the United States: the PRO has not shown that the funds reached by such freezes pay for attacks here or the propaganda urging them.

The FBI's Level Up program contacts victims directly. Sources: [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13].

points.title: Disrupting investment scams helps protect mental health.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Disrupting investment scams helps protect mental health.

  • Because Stablecoins carry proceeds from scams aimed at ordinary Americans. In 2023, the Justice Department seized Tether from a scam network and said: “Through this significant seizure, we disrupted the financial infrastructure of an organized network of scammers who stole millions from victims across the United States.” [11]
  • Because The harm reaches health. The FBI reports: “Some victims were so emotionally impacted by the scam, they were referred to the FBI Victim Services Division and provided direct support or suicide intervention.” [13]
  • Because FBI warnings have stopped further payments: “these victims did not make any further investments.” [13]
  • Because The schemes reach ordinary adults: “They target victims from all walks of life” [13].
  • So The bill’s required tracing standards and blocking duties strengthen tools for finding these networks and cutting off their funds. Disrupting scams before they take more from victims helps prevent the severe distress they cause. Protecting mental health gives [NAME] a personal security reason to favor those controls.
points.con_html:
Response The scam examples do not connect the bill's tracing standards to earlier detection of scam networks.

  • Because Compliance with a freezing order still depends on identified targets. The order must specify “the payment stablecoins or accounts subject to blocking with reasonable particularity” [3].
  • Because FinCEN's April 2026 proposal for issuers' crime-control programs, which is separate from Section 9, states: “FinCEN is not proposing to require a PPSI as part of an AML/CFT program to monitor secondary market activity” [6].
  • So This leaves the duty to block identified funds unanswered. It challenges the PRO's step from issuer duties to “finding these networks”: on this record, the tracing standards are unwritten and the proposed program rule does not require that monitoring.

It does not propose requiring issuers, as part of an AML/CFT program, to monitor secondary-market activity or file SARs on secondary-market transactions, and it requests comment. Section 9(d) rulemaking is separate. Sources: [6].

points.title: Disrupting sexual blackmail helps protect health and personal safety.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Disrupting sexual blackmail helps protect health and personal safety.

  • Because Sexual blackmail demands money under threats to expose intimate images. It can reach ordinary adults: “These schemes can target anyone” [19].
  • Because Since April 2023, the FBI has also seen victims targeted with fake explicit images made from ordinary photos: “the use of fake images or videos created from content posted on a victim’s social media page” [19].
  • Because The threats can be deadly: “financially motivated sextortion has led to an alarming number of victim suicides.” [19]
  • Because Services offered to sexual blackmailers take stablecoins. Elliptic found a Huione Guarantee merchant that “specializes in the laundering of sextortion scams” [20]. On that marketplace, “Payments are advertised as being accepted primarily in the USDT stablecoin” [20].
  • Because Those payments offer a way to disrupt the crime: “investigators and compliance teams are able to proactively detect and disrupt USDT payments by using blockchain analytics.” [20]
  • Because Suspicious-activity reports help investigators act. FinCEN says they “may aid law enforcement in disrupting these actors and prevent further victimization.” [19]
  • So The bill’s tracing standards and enforceable freezing duties strengthen this route for finding blackmailers and obstructing their money flows. Stopping coercion that drives victims to despair and suicide serves [NAME]’s interest in health and personal safety.
points.con_html:
Response The blackmail example does not establish that the bill's reporting and tracing duties would reach the cited network's payments.

  • Because Section 8 makes U.S. trading depend on compliance “with the terms of any lawful order” [3]. That condition addresses issuer compliance with an identified order; it does not itself identify sexual blackmail or its victims.
  • Because The PRO relies on suspicious-activity reports, but in its April 2026 proposal “FinCEN is also not proposing to require PPSIs to file SARs on secondary market transactions” [6]. Payments between marketplace users would ordinarily fall in that category.
  • So This leaves enforceable freezing of identified funds unanswered. It challenges the step from issuer reporting and tracing to finding blackmailers. The proposal is not final, and Section 9's standards remain to be written.

It does not propose requiring issuers, as part of an AML/CFT program, to monitor secondary-market activity or file SARs on secondary-market transactions, and it requests comment. Section 9(d) rulemaking is separate. Sources: [6].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose S.1582?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect The bill would create a national system of federal and state approval for stablecoin issuers and encourage wider use in payments. Stablecoins are digital tokens meant to exchange for a fixed amount of money. “Stablecoins could be issued by banks and credit unions (through subsidiaries) or nonbanks.” [1] The framework would remove a barrier to wider entry: major financial firms previously “largely stayed away from them, put off by regulatory uncertainty and crypto’s association with illicit transactions.” [21] These tokens would reach household payment money: they are “used as a substitute for cash or bank transaction accounts.” [22]

points.title: Moving everyday money into uninsured stablecoins would put funds needed for medical care at risk of loss or delay.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Moving everyday money into uninsured stablecoins would put funds needed for medical care at risk of loss or delay.

  • Because Stablecoins issued under this framework “are not federally insured.” [1]
  • Because Backing a $1 token with reserves does not guarantee it can be resold for $1 where ordinary customers trade. Researchers identify the bill’s “omission of any reference to maintaining par-value exchange in the secondary market (where most stablecoin users actually transact)” [23].
  • Because If an issuer fails, money can be frozen. The bill would “allow a bankruptcy court to issue automatic stays on stablecoin redemptions.” [1] This means blocking exchanges of tokens for money.
  • Because Available money matters for ordinary Americans’ care. The Federal Reserve reports: “Twenty-eight percent of adults went without some form of medical care in 2024 because they could not afford it” [24].
  • So Wider use would expose more household payment funds to losses or freezes when people need money for medicine and treatment.
  • So Protecting access to care gives [NAME] a health reason to oppose this shift.
  • Note A claim on reserve assets in bankruptcy does not make money spendable while redemptions are frozen.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The researchers cited by the PRO state the Act substantially improves reserve quality and disclosure. The bill also directs operational and IT risk rules. Sources: [23], [3].

Evidence note: Brookings says that without interest holders have incentives to minimize their holdings, and that faster payments let a given volume of stablecoins support more payments. Governor Waller said in February 2025 that retail stablecoin use was very limited, that significant retail impact would probably take years, and also that merchants could have an incentive to accept stablecoins if they reduce fees or attract customers. Sources: [22], [25].

Evidence note: Waller describes limited retail use and says a significant retail impact would probably take years. Below-par resales and bankruptcy stays were possible before this bill. These facts limit scale and timing and identify the baseline; they do not by themselves refute the PRO's conditional exposure route. Sources: [25], [23], [26].

points.title: Wider use would make health-care funds depend on shared networks that can fail or be attacked.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Wider use would make health-care funds depend on shared networks that can fail or be attacked.

  • Because The bill includes public blockchains—shared computer records used to move tokens—among the systems its rules address: “accepted communications protocols and blockchains, permissioned or public.” [3]
  • Because Network problems can block access even when an issuer holds its reserves. Researchers explain that “if the underlying network is congested, attacked, or otherwise unable to process transactions, transfers and issuer operations may be delayed or fail.” [23]
  • Because Growth can also make attacks more rewarding. For Ethereum, one public network used by stablecoins, researchers explain: “The cost to mount the attack does not scale with the economic value transacted on Ethereum, but the expected reward does.” [23]
  • So Wider adoption would put more household funds on these networks and increase the rewards for attacking them.
  • So Given the cost barriers to care in point 1, losing access to payment money threatens treatment. Avoiding this added source of interruption gives [NAME] a health reason to oppose.
  • Note Holding financial reserves does not by itself keep the network processing payments.
points.con_html:
Response The network evidence does not establish that the bill would increase interruptions to ordinary Americans’ care.

  • Because The technical paper sets out risks under assumed growth. It describes its scope as “a policy-oriented risk analysis rather than an assessment of stablecoins’ desirability, long-run adoption prospects, or impact on global currency arrangements.” [23] Its failure scenarios do not establish how added payment activity would expose household care funds.
  • Because Household payment use requires steps beyond approving issuers. A Federal Reserve governor explains that it requires “a substantial number of consumers to shift their preferences toward using stablecoins and a significant number of businesses to make necessary investments to receive payments via stablecoins.” [25]
  • So A network vulnerability and a larger reward for an attack do not establish the missing link: that the added activity would make households depend on the affected network for money needed for treatment.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The researchers cited by the PRO state the Act substantially improves reserve quality and disclosure. The bill also directs operational and IT risk rules. Sources: [23], [3].

points.title: The bill would lend credibility to tokens whose users face fraud losses without adding a required complaints process.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill would lend credibility to tokens whose users face fraud losses without adding a required complaints process.

  • Because A consumer advocate warns that the bill would “create a regulatory imprimatur for stablecoins without removing the dangers associated with them” [21]. The new approval system can encourage trust while payment risks remain.
  • Because Stablecoins already carry scam proceeds. A June 2025 Justice Department complaint alleges “USDT traceable to cryptocurrency confidence scams” [27]. USDT is identified in the same complaint as Tether, a stablecoin.
  • Because The bill itself does not require a process for investigating customers’ transfer complaints. The Consumer Policy Center finds: “Unlike the law for other payment systems, the Act does not require issuers to establish a procedure that requires issuers to investigate consumer complaints.” [28]
  • So The new credibility would draw household money into a market used by scammers, without requiring issuers to investigate customers’ missing funds.
  • Because Losses that make essential bills unaffordable create financial strain. A review of U.S. longitudinal studies finds: “There is a consistent, positive association between financial strain and depression in the United States.” [29]
  • So Fraud losses that leave users struggling to pay bills carry a documented mental-health concern. Protecting mental health gives [NAME] a reason to oppose promoting this exposure.
points.con_html:
Response The evidence does not show that issuer approval would increase fraud losses through the route the PRO describes.

  • Because The cited complaint describes a scam built on false investment accounts: “the apps are created and controlled by the perpetrators” [27]. That deception rests on fake apps, and the PRO does not connect lawful issuer approval to increased belief in them.
  • Because The missing new complaints rule must be assessed against existing rights. Section 6 says: “Nothing in this Act may be construed to modify or otherwise affect any right or remedy under any Federal consumer financial law” [3]. An omitted new process does not itself show a change in fraud losses.
  • So The warning about official credibility, the cited scam, and the omitted complaints rule do not establish increased fraud losses under this framework. The depression review cannot supply that step.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The bill bars marketing a coin so that a reasonable person sees it as U.S.-guaranteed or approved, and requires issuers to be able to block, freeze and reject impermissible transactions. Sources: [3].

points.title: Greater links between stablecoins and banks would spread risks to the health-care budgets of people who never use crypto.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Greater links between stablecoins and banks would spread risks to the health-care budgets of people who never use crypto.

  • Because The bill permits reserves in uninsured bank deposits. A Brookings analysis explains: “Moreover, allowing stablecoins to hold uninsured bank deposits creates direct two-way interconnections between the risk of banks and the risk of stablecoins.” [30]
  • Because A rush to exchange tokens for dollars can drain otherwise sound banks. “Similarly, a stablecoin issuer deemed at risk of breaking the buck could lead to a rapid withdrawal of deposits at banks that otherwise were sound.” [22]
  • Because Bank-payment data show this link already operates. Studying banks serving one issuer, New York Fed researchers find: “Stablecoins directly transmit liquidity shocks to the banking system” [31]. These are sudden demands for ready cash.
  • So Expanding stablecoin use would enlarge a route from token runs to banking stress, beyond the people who own tokens.
  • Because Financial crises reach ordinary households’ incomes and savings. In 2008, “millions of Americans lost their homes, jobs, and retirement savings—even those who had never received a subprime loan or made risky investments.” [14] This shows how a crisis can reach households, not the expected size of a stablecoin-related shock.
  • So Expanding this route for financial shocks puts household money for care at risk and exposes nonusers to the financial strain linked to depression. Those health stakes give [NAME] a reason to oppose even without owning stablecoins.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Federal guidance in March 2025 reaffirmed permission to hold deposits backing stablecoins in certain circumstances. The NY Fed study reports partner banks retain larger reserve balances to manage liquidity exposure. The bill directs diversification rules and lets deposit insurers limit reserve deposits on safety grounds. Sources: [32], [31], [3].

pages.description: S.1582 creates federal rules for "stablecoins" — digital coins an issuer must redeem for a fixed dollar value. Only permitted, regulated companies may issue them, and each coin must be fully backed one-to-one by cash or similar safe assets that issuers may not lend out.
