directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.1582?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on July 17, 2025, the bill would add national rules for licensing and overseeing payment stablecoin issuers: companies that create digital payment tokens redeemable for a fixed sum. “This bill establishes a regulatory framework for payment stablecoins (digital assets which an issuer must redeem for a fixed value).” [1] Existing state oversight typically imposed “more limited requirements than the bills propose.” [2]

points.title: It strengthens the state’s tools for finding and cutting off funds for terrorists, cartels, and other security threats.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It strengthens the state’s tools for finding and cutting off funds for terrorists, cartels, and other security threats.

  • Because Stablecoins already serve these threats: “Evidence points to increased use for terrorist financing and money laundering.” [3]
  • Because Permitted issuers must check their account holders and report suspicious transactions: “identification and verification of account holders with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer” [4]; “monitoring and reporting of any suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation” [4].
  • Because Issuers must certify programs aimed at preventing “facilitating money laundering for cartels and organizations designated as foreign terrorist organizations” [4]. Failure to submit the certification lets regulators “revoke the approval of the payment stablecoin issuer under this section.” [4]
  • Because The bill bars officers and directors convicted of felonies involving “cybercrime, money laundering, financing of terrorism, or financial fraud” [4]. Federal licensing also weighs the “competence, experience, and integrity of the officers, directors, and principal shareholders” [4].
  • Because It makes the ability and willingness to obey federal blocking orders a condition of issuance: “A permitted payment stablecoin issuer may issue payment stablecoins only if the issuer has the technological capability to comply, and will comply, with the terms of any lawful order.” [4] These orders require issuers to “seize, freeze, burn, or prevent the transfer of payment stablecoins issued by the person” [4].
  • Because Treasury can act against foreign issuers that defy those orders, after notice, by “prohibiting digital asset service providers from facilitating secondary trading of payment stablecoins issued by the foreign payment stablecoin issuer in the United States.” [4]
  • Because The foreign-issuer registration review checks “whether the foreign payment stablecoin issuer presents illicit finance risks to the United States.” [4] Registered issuers must “consent to United States jurisdiction relating to the enforcement of this Act.” [4]
  • Because That foreign-issuer route excludes countries under sweeping U.S. sanctions or designated as major money-laundering risks: the country must be “not subject to comprehensive economic sanctions by the United States or in a jurisdiction that the Secretary of the Treasury has determined to be a jurisdiction of primary money laundering concern.” [4]
  • Because Treasury must research better detection methods, and its financial-crime agency must issue guidance and rules on “Standards for payment stablecoin issuers' systems and practices to monitor transactions on blockchains, digital asset mixing services, tumblers, or other similar services” [4]. These services can hide who sends or receives money.
  • So Licensing checks, reporting, blocking technology, and access to U.S. trading platforms give the state ways to trace and interrupt threat financing. Better detection rules extend those defenses as methods change. That strengthens the country’s ability to protect its citizens.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not establish added ability to find threat-linked funds soon enough to interrupt them.

  • Because The bill requires “identification and verification of account holders with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, high-value transactions, and appropriate enhanced due diligence” [4]. The tracing problem extends to later transfers: “a stablecoin issuer cannot easily know or control who will ultimately be using its stablecoins after issuance.” [5]
  • Because Finding funds soon enough is a separate problem from having authority to freeze them: “current practices to block and freeze accounts may be too slow and too late to prevent illicit transactions” [5]. Section 9 requires research and later rules on detection; it calls for evaluating “Improvements in the ability of financial institutions to detect illicit activity involving digital assets.” [4]
  • Because FinCEN's April 2026 proposal keeps secondary-market duties for blocking and lawful orders, but states: “FinCEN is not proposing to require a PPSI as part of an AML/CFT program to monitor secondary market activity” [6]. The proposal is not final and is separate from Section 9.
  • So This leaves the freezing duty, management screening, and foreign-issuer conditions unanswered. It challenges the PRO's inference that licensing and reporting rules improve the timely detection of threat-linked transfers after issuance.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: FinCEN and OFAC's April 2026 proposed rule would apply secondary-market obligations to blocking, freezing and rejecting impermissible transactions and to complying with lawful orders. It does not propose requiring issuers, as part of an AML/CFT program, to monitor secondary-market activity or file SARs on secondary-market transactions, and it requests comment. Section 9(d) rulemaking is separate. Sources: [6].

Evidence note: FinCEN's 2019 guidance treats administrators and exchangers as money transmitters with AML duties. Tether reported assisting a $23 million Garantex freeze in March 2025. Issuer smart contracts process on-chain transfers, and Treasury's March 2026 report says analytics can detect suspicious patterns. FinCEN's April 2026 proposal keeps secondary-market duties for blocking and lawful orders but not for AML-program monitoring or SARs. Sources: [7], [8], [9], [10], [6].

points.title: It limits weak reserves and poor oversight that can turn mass withdrawals into a wider financial crisis.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It limits weak reserves and poor oversight that can turn mass withdrawals into a wider financial crisis.

  • Because Risky reserves expose payment money to a run—a rush to withdraw: “Private money backed by risky assets with inadequate capital would be vulnerable to destabilizing runs and lose its ability to function as a medium of exchange.” [3]
  • Because Forced sales can spread the damage: an issuer in crisis “might be forced to sell off its treasuries in panic, resulting in broader damage and loss of confidence to the financial system.” [11]
  • Because The bill requires full backing with cash or other assets readily sold or withdrawn: “Permitted issuers must maintain reserves backing the stablecoin on a one-to-one basis using U.S. currency or other similarly liquid assets, as specified.” [1]
  • Because It limits the use of backing assets for other purposes: “Reserves required under paragraph (1)(A) may not be pledged, rehypothecated, or reused by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, either directly or indirectly” [4]. The listed exceptions cover specified reserve transactions, custody, and raising cash for redemptions.
  • Because Regulators must set “reserve asset diversification, including deposit concentration at banking institutions, and interest rate risk management standards” [4]. These address exposure to one bank and losses from changes in interest rates.
  • Because Reserve reports make the backing open to checks: issuers must “publish the monthly composition of the issuer's reserves on the website of the issuer” [4], and reports must be “examined by a registered public accounting firm.” [4]
  • Because Federal examinations assess risks to “the stability of the financial system of the United States” [4]. For issuers under federal enforcement, regulators can order them to “take affirmative action to correct the conditions resulting from any such violation or practice.” [4]
  • Because State regimes face federal certification against national requirements: the approval test is that the regime “meets or exceeds the standards and requirements described in subsection (a)” [4]. In unusual and urgent circumstances, federal authorities can “take an enforcement action against a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer or an institution-affiliated party of such issuer for violations of this Act during such unusual and exigent circumstances.” [4]
  • Because Foreign issuers using the bill’s U.S. access route must face comparable regulation, including reserve rules: Treasury must find a regime “comparable to the regulatory and supervisory regime established under this Act, including, in particular, the requirements under section 4(a).” [4] Registration review also considers “whether the foreign payment stablecoin presents a risk to the financial stability of the United States” [4].
  • So Full backing, limits on reserve risks and use, and enforceable oversight address the conditions that cause runs and forced sales. Reducing those routes to a financial crisis protects the stable U.S. economy [NAME] values.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO leaves out the cash-shortage mechanism that connects its permitted reserves to the panic selling it claims to reduce.

  • Because The bill allows reserves held as bank deposits and cash borrowed against Treasury securities: “funds held as demand deposits” [4]; “money received under repurchase agreements, with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer acting as a seller of securities” [4]. A repurchase agreement is short-term borrowing against securities.
  • Because A promise to repay with these assets differs from cash available during stress. The PRO's source explains that “uninsured deposits are risky and illiquid” [12] and create “direct two-way interconnections between the risk of banks and the risk of stablecoins.” [12]
  • Because Borrowing to meet withdrawals also creates a feedback problem: “While repo transactions are generally low risk, the provisions would allow stablecoin issuers to borrow, creating leverage. In periods when redemptions were increasing, this could prompt even more redemptions.” [5] Leverage means using borrowed money.
  • Because The bill directs regulators to set capital, liquidity, and deposit-concentration rules. Their substance matters: “Without appropriate standards to reduce runs and limit interconnections, stablecoins could create the type of fire sale dynamics from prime money market mutual funds (MMFs) during the Global Financial Crisis.” [12]
  • So This leaves the backing duty, limits on reuse, and public reports unanswered. It challenges the further claim that these rules address the conditions that cause runs: they do not show how cash stays available when deposits freeze or borrowing fuels further withdrawals, and the required standards remain to be written.

points.title: It protects payment funds when an issuer or a firm safeguarding assets fails.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It protects payment funds when an issuer or a firm safeguarding assets fails.

  • Because Covered custodians—firms safeguarding stablecoin reserves, coins used as collateral, or keys used to issue coins—must protect customer property from their own creditors: “take such steps as are appropriate to protect the payment stablecoins, private keys, cash, and other property of a customer from the claims of creditors of the person.” [4] The bill’s general rule is that the property “shall be segregated from and not be commingled with the assets of the person.” [4]
  • Because In an issuer’s failure, coin holders have first claims on required reserves. Their claims rank “over the claims of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and any other holder of claims against the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, with respect to required payment stablecoin reserves” [4].
  • Because If reserves fall short, holders’ unpaid claims also get priority on the issuer’s other assets to cover missing required reserves: “shall have first priority over any other claim” [4].
  • Because On the issuer’s request, if the court finds reserves available for payments to similarly placed holders, it must try to approve distributions promptly: “the court shall use best efforts to enter a final order to begin distributions under this paragraph not later than 14 days after the date of the required hearing.” [4]
  • Because These protections serve access to payment money after failure: “Reserve assets of a stablecoin should be segregated and prioritized in bankruptcy, so that holders can still access their payment stablecoins if a stablecoin issuer were to fail.” [3]
  • So Protecting payment assets and giving holders a route to recover them limits the disruption a failed firm causes to households, businesses, and commerce. That protects national economic stability.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO's route from creditor priority to less payment disruption skips a funding obstacle created by that same priority.

  • Because When required reserves are missing, section 11 puts holders' claims ahead of the expenses of running the bankruptcy. Bankruptcy lawyers explain that these claims would outrank “general administrative claims relating to the estate representative preserving the bankruptcy estate” [13]. Their warning concerns the repayment process itself: “The subordination of administrative claims to the shortfall claims may increase the likelihood that the estate will become administratively insolvent or that a reorganization of the debtor issuer will not be feasible.” [13] This means too little money to pay for the process or keep the firm operating.
  • Because Excluding reserves from the issuer's bankruptcy estate does not release them for payments. The bill expressly freezes “the redemption of payment stablecoins” [4]. Its target is a best-efforts order to begin distributions “not later than 14 days after the date of the required hearing.” [4] This is neither a deadline measured from failure nor a deadline for completing payouts.
  • Because The custody rule also has a cash exception. Bank deposits held as reserves “shall not be subject to any requirement relating to the separation of such cash from the property of the applicable depository institution” [4]. The general segregation rule therefore does not shield that cash from the bank's own failure.
  • So The PRO moves from stronger legal claims to better access to payment cash without resolving the obstacle to funding recovery, the cash-deposit exception, or the statutory pause. It has not shown that its priority rules deliver the less disruptive recovery it claims.

points.title: It requires defenses against technical failures and cyberattacks on payments.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It requires defenses against technical failures and cyberattacks on payments.

  • Because Stablecoins “could undermine the safety of payments if their operations are not robust to a range of operational and cyber threats.” [3]
  • Because Regulators must establish “appropriate operational, compliance, and information technology risk management principles-based requirements and standards” [4].
  • So Requiring issuers to manage these risks strengthens defenses against failures and attacks that interrupt payments. Reliable payments help keep U.S. commerce working under threat.
points.con_html:
Response A general duty to set issuer standards does not establish an added defense against failures of the shared networks that carry payments.

  • Because The bill directs regulators to set “appropriate operational, compliance, and information technology risk management principles-based requirements and standards” [4]. That instruction does not specify a new recovery method or how an issuer would restore a failed shared blockchain—the network recording its payments.
  • Because Analysis identifies the missing mechanism, asking whether coins could move to another blockchain after an outage: “Mechanisms to protect users in these situations exist in traditional payments, and work is ongoing to develop them for stablecoins based on permissionless blockchains.” [5] Such blockchains let people join without an operator's approval.
  • So This leaves the protection from issuer-level standards unanswered. It challenges the claim's reach to outages on shared networks, which these standards are not shown to improve.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: FTC Safeguards rules cover wire transferors, and New York licensees had cyber recovery duties. Sources: [14], [15].

points.title: It limits the spread of stablecoin trouble into banking and ordinary commerce.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It limits the spread of stablecoin trouble into banking and ordinary commerce.

  • Because Public companies mainly outside finance, and companies they wholly or mostly own, need unanimous approval from the bill’s federal review committee before issuing stablecoins. The finding must include that issuance “will not pose a material risk to the safety and soundness of the United States banking system, the financial stability of the United States, or the Deposit Insurance Fund” [4].
  • Because This review targets the spread of financial trouble: “This provision aims to separate damage to the financial side of a large company from spreading to its non-financial functions.” [11]
  • Because The bill also narrows the issuer’s business: “Issuers’ activities are restricted to offering and redeeming stablecoins and ancillary activities.” [12] Ancillary activities are supporting work, such as managing reserves and safeguarding assets.
  • So A safety gate for these commercial groups, together with limits on issuer activities, restricts routes through which payment troubles spread across the economy. That serves [NAME]’s concern for a stable country.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Brookings says the GENIUS Act does not strictly protect the separation of banking and commerce. The activity limit applies to the issuer, and the committee test applies to public companies. Sources: [12], [4].

points.title: It limits corporate barriers that can put payments under concentrated private control.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It limits corporate barriers that can put payments under concentrated private control.

  • Because Such barriers threaten economic stability: “Serious risks to economic and monetary stability could arise if nonfinancial firms can take advantage of existing private data from their platforms or raise the costs of switching to other payment products.” [12]
  • Because The bill bars issuers from forcing customers to buy another paid product, or to avoid a competitor: an issuer “may not provide services to a customer on the condition that the customer obtain an additional paid product or service from the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, or any of its subsidiaries, or agree to not obtain an additional product or service from a competitor.” [4]
  • Because It also directs regulators to assess, and lets them set, standards to “promote compatibility and interoperability” [4], so payment systems can work with each other.
  • So The ban protects customers’ access to competing services, while the standards power addresses barriers between payment systems. Keeping money and commerce from being locked inside one company’s services protects economic and monetary stability.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO treats access to competing products as evidence that users can move their payment money between competing networks.

  • Because Its source identifies a distinct source of concentration: “the system is more valuable the more participants there are” [12]. It also identifies the risk from firms that “raise the costs of switching to other payment products.” [12] Neither problem requires a forced sale of another product.
  • Because The bill bars requiring an “additional paid product or service” [4] and an agreement “to not obtain an additional product or service from a competitor.” [4] These sales conditions differ from the cost and technical ability to move money out of a network.
  • Because Section 12 says regulators “shall assess and, if necessary, may” [4] prescribe standards for systems to work together. It supplies a power to set standards, rather than a requirement that issuers accept transfers across their networks.
  • So The PRO has not connected its sales ban and standards power to lower switching barriers. Permission to buy a competing service does not establish that payment balances can move there. Its conclusion about preventing money and commerce from being locked inside a platform skips that step.

points.title: It removes issuer-paid interest as an incentive to move money out of banks.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 It removes issuer-paid interest as an incentive to move money out of banks.

  • Because The bill forbids both permitted and foreign issuers to pay interest or yield solely for holding or using their coins: “No permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer shall pay the holder of any payment stablecoin any form of interest or yield” [4].
  • Because Paying interest can pull funds from the banking system: “It also could draw funds away from bank deposits that underpin lending to households and businesses and are a key transmission channel for monetary policy.” [3]
  • So Removing this incentive protects bank funding for lending and a channel through which the central bank steadies the economy. Both support the national stability [NAME] values.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: CRS reports that much retail stablecoin use occurs through exchanges, that GENIUS does not explicitly prevent exchanges from paying rewards on coins they hold, that many do, and that Circle pays part of its reserve interest to Coinbase. CRS also says the issuer is prohibited from paying interest in a direct issuer-to-customer model, that the restriction would presumably apply to self-custody, and that 'holder' is undefined. Coinbase attributes part of its USDC balance growth to its rewards program. AAF says issuers can effectively circumvent the ban through exchanges or third parties. Sources: [16], [17], [18].

points.title: It supports U.S. capacity to develop and govern strategic payment technology at home.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 It supports U.S. capacity to develop and govern strategic payment technology at home.

  • Because A clear domestic framework supports development: “These measures lay out a missing legal framework for stablecoins” [19]; “These are reasonable guardrails that should encourage continued growth in this space.” [19]
  • Because Losing expertise abroad threatens that capacity: “Industry brain drain is a real risk to our leadership in technology and financial services” [19].
  • Because Payment technology affects state power: “As financial systems determine geopolitical leverage, sanctions enforcement, data sovereignty, and the global role of the U.S. dollar, competitiveness in this area is essential.” [20]
  • So A workable U.S. route for firms and expertise strengthens the country’s capacity to build and oversee technology central to its financial power. That supports a state able to defend its citizens.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: OCC confirmed in March 2025 that certain stablecoin activities are permissible and rescinded its nonobjection requirement. The bill also has a route for foreign issuers. Sources: [21], [4].

points.title: It strengthens dollar-based payments against rival systems designed to escape U.S. financial controls.
points.pro_html:
Point 9 It strengthens dollar-based payments against rival systems designed to escape U.S. financial controls.

  • Because The bill supports wider use of digital dollars: “The passage of the GENIUS Act is expected to lead to rapid growth in the circulation of bank-issued dollar stablecoins.” [22]
  • Because Rivals are building alternatives: “U.S. competitors are pushing alternative payment systems that are designed to weaken the dollar’s influence and U.S. centrality within the international financial system.” [23]
  • Because That shift affects the state’s ability to apply financial pressure: “Russia, the BRICS bloc, and sanctioned states like Iran and Venezuela are also exploring digital assets to skirt U.S. financial controls.” [23]
  • So Expanding regulated dollar payments helps keep international finance within U.S. reach. Preserving that influence strengthens the state’s ability to use financial restrictions against security threats.
points.con_html:
Response More dollar-denominated payments do not by themselves put the channels carrying those payments within U.S. enforcement reach.

  • Because Dollar use and avoidance of U.S. controls already coexisted. The PRO's source reports “98 percent of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar” [23] and explains that “Stablecoins can bypass traditional financial monitoring points via peer-to-peer or decentralized finance transactions” [23]. These are direct transfers or transactions through software rather than a conventional financial firm.
  • Because That enforcement problem includes finding funds, not just ordering a freeze. Before the bill, the Justice Department alleged that Garantex changed wallet addresses daily “to make it difficult for U.S.-based cryptocurrency exchanges to identify and block transactions with Garantex accounts.” [24]
  • Because The bill's section 3 restrictions on issuance and sales exclude “any transaction by means of a software or hardware wallet that facilitates an individual's own custody of digital assets.” [4] Its separate freezing powers still depend on locating the funds to be frozen.
  • So The PRO has not shown that growth in regulated dollar tokens replaces rival payment channels with transactions the United States can newly detect and stop. Currency choice alone does not establish that added sanctions power.

points.title: It supports demand that lowers the government’s short-term borrowing costs.
points.pro_html:
Point 10 It supports demand that lowers the government’s short-term borrowing costs.

  • Because The bill is “expected to lead to rapid growth in the circulation of bank-issued dollar stablecoins.” [22] It allows “short-dated Treasury bills” [25] among required reserves.
  • Because That growth creates a source of demand for government debt: “The widespread adoption of well-regulated dollar-backed stablecoins would also drive increased demand for U.S. debt” [26].
  • Because A study published by the Bank for International Settlements finds: “Inflows into stablecoins reduce three-month US Treasury bill yields” [27]. Yields are the interest rates on this government debt.
  • So Supporting this demand helps the state borrow at lower short-term rates. Money saved on interest is available to defend citizens and meet national emergencies, giving [NAME] a security-based reason to favor the framework.
points.con_html:
Response The price study does not establish that this bill creates additional public resources for defense and emergencies.

  • Because Reserve purchases are not the same as extra demand across all buyers. Analysis explains that “other forms of payments media, such as cash, demand deposits, and MMMFs may shrink, reducing the demand for Treasury bills.” [5] These are cash, bank balances, and money market mutual funds that already support Treasury demand.
  • Because Lower borrowing rates are also not the same as more public money. Replacing currency shifts earnings to private issuers: “For stablecoins, the issuers get the seigniorage, whereas for currency, the seigniorage accrues to the U.S. Treasury.” [5] Seigniorage is the income from issuing money and investing its backing. The analysis concludes that “the net impact on debt service costs is likely to be negligible” [5].
  • So The PRO has not established extra federal resources after the shift in demand and public earnings. A measured fall in short-term yields does not fill that gap in its security-funding claim.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose S.1582?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect The bill creates a national licensing system for payment stablecoins: private digital tokens redeemable for a fixed sum. “Stablecoins could be issued by banks and credit unions (through subsidiaries) or nonbanks.” [25] Compared with the law in force on July 17, 2025, it puts permission for bank involvement into statute: “The GENIUS Act codified permission for banks to issue their own stablecoins and perform other activities, thereby strengthening certain linkages between industries.” [28] AEI's analysis of GENIUS and the House's stablecoin bill predicts wider use: “The passage of either bills will likely accelerate the integration of private stablecoins into the retail banking environment.” [29]

points.title: It expands payment channels that terrorists, sanctions evaders, and criminal networks can use beyond bank identity checks.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It expands payment channels that terrorists, sanctions evaders, and criminal networks can use beyond bank identity checks.

  • Because Stablecoins can move outside the places where banks check customers: “Stablecoins can bypass traditional financial monitoring points via peer-to-peer or decentralized finance transactions, making them attractive for illicit use.” [23]
  • Because These threats already use stablecoins. Of Tether's USDT, Bloomberg reports: “Its USDT coins have been seized and forfeited in cases involving fraud, terrorist financing, sanctions violations and other criminal activity.” [30]
  • Note The bill requires issuer checks and powers to freeze funds, but coins can move beyond the issuer's direct customer relationships: “Once purchased, however, the stablecoins may be transferred to decentralized wallets, where there is less control over who holds and transacts with them.” [31]
  • Because Freezing funds case by case also burdens public authorities. The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) warns that “employing a request-based approach for billions of transactions with pseudonymous addresses would quickly overwhelm the capacity of those authorities.” [32] These are addresses whose users' real names are not shown.
  • So Wider use expands the payments authorities must police without putting an identity check on every transfer. That makes it harder to stop funding for threats to Americans and enforce U.S. sanctions.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: FinCEN and OFAC's April 2026 proposed rule would apply secondary-market obligations to blocking, freezing and rejecting impermissible transactions and to complying with lawful orders. It does not propose requiring issuers, as part of an AML/CFT program, to monitor secondary-market activity or file SARs on secondary-market transactions, and it requests comment. Section 9(d) rulemaking is separate. Sources: [6].

Evidence note: FinCEN's 2019 guidance treats administrators and exchangers as money transmitters with AML duties. Tether reported assisting a $23 million Garantex freeze in March 2025. Issuer smart contracts process on-chain transfers, and Treasury's March 2026 report says analytics can detect suspicious patterns. FinCEN's April 2026 proposal keeps secondary-market duties for blocking and lawful orders but not for AML-program monitoring or SARs. Sources: [7], [8], [9], [10], [6].

Brief context note: Under Section 5, a substantially complete federal application not decided within 120 days is deemed approved. A federal regulator must evaluate each application, and approved issuers face examination. Before the bill, nonbank stablecoin supervision was primarily at the state level, and OCC rescinded its nonobjection requirement for its supervised institutions in March 2025. Section 5(h) preempts state licensing requirements for federally approved issuers. Sources: [25], [4], [33], [21].

points.title: It gives foreign issuers a place in the expanded payment system without requiring a thorough check for hidden control by adversaries.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It gives foreign issuers a place in the expanded payment system without requiring a thorough check for hidden control by adversaries.

  • Because Section 18 creates a route for foreign coins through approved home-country rules and registration with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, a federal bank regulator: “A foreign payment stablecoin issuer may offer or sell payment stablecoins using a digital asset service provider if the foreign payment stablecoin issuer is registered with the Comptroller.” [4]
  • Because CSIS, a policy research group, identifies a gap in that route: “The act includes a pathway for foreign payment stablecoin issuers (FPSIs) but does not require rigorous screening of foreign governance structures.” [20]
  • Note The bill requires the home country to be “not subject to comprehensive economic sanctions by the United States” [4] and directs registration review to consider “whether the foreign payment stablecoin issuer presents illicit finance risks to the United States.” [4] Those checks do not establish who ultimately controls a firm based elsewhere. CSIS explains: “Insufficient oversight of ultimate ownership and controlling interests might allow adversaries to influence an FPSI, creating national security risks.” [20]
  • So As the bill draws stablecoins into ordinary finance, this route exposes more U.S. payments to hidden foreign influence over infrastructure the country needs to remain secure.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Bloomberg described USDT as widely available on U.S. exchanges before the vote. Section 18 requires comparable regulation, registration, reporting and examination, and allows revocation on reasonable grounds of illicit finance risk. Sources: [30], [4].

Brief context note: Under Section 5, a substantially complete federal application not decided within 120 days is deemed approved. A federal regulator must evaluate each application, and approved issuers face examination. Before the bill, nonbank stablecoin supervision was primarily at the state level, and OCC rescinded its nonobjection requirement for its supervised institutions in March 2025. Section 5(h) preempts state licensing requirements for federally approved issuers. Sources: [25], [4], [33], [21].

points.title: It makes essential payments a more valuable target for attacks on networks outside an issuer's control.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It makes essential payments a more valuable target for attacks on networks outside an issuer's control.

  • Because The bill bars rejecting an issuer simply for using an open network: “The issuance of a payment stablecoin on an open, public, or decentralized network shall not be a valid ground for denial of an application received under subsection (a).” [4] A public blockchain is a shared transaction record run by network participants.
  • Because Regulating an issuer does not put that whole network under its control. Research on coins that meet GENIUS requirements explains: “Although some risks are in the control of the stablecoin issuer, many are not.” [9]
  • Because On Ethereum, one public blockchain, growth increases the reward for attacks: “As stablecoin transaction volume rises, the opportunity for double spends in the stablecoin increases, while there is not necessarily a corresponding increase in the punishment for conducting an attack.” [9] A double spend means spending the same tokens twice.
  • Because Network failure can stop payments even when the backing assets remain safe: “A disruption to the functioning of the blockchain will disrupt the execution of stablecoin transactions that are dependent on the functioning of the blockchain.” [9]
  • So Expanding everyday payments on such networks raises both the rewards for attackers and the economic stakes of an outage. Keeping essential transactions working is part of keeping the country secure and stable.
points.con_html:
Response The Ethereum attack scenario does not establish that the bill makes essential U.S. payments depend on networks with that weakness.

  • Because The technical study analyzes risks under assumed growth; it does not forecast adoption. Its authors state: “Our work is intended as a policy-oriented risk analysis rather than an assessment of stablecoins’ desirability, long-run adoption prospects, or impact on global currency arrangements.” [9]
  • So The PRO joins a general forecast of market growth to a specific network's attack incentives. It has not established the step from that growth to dependence of essential U.S. payments on such networks.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Section 5 retains denial for unsafe or unsound activities, and Section 4 directs operational and IT risk standards. Sources: [4].

Brief context note: Under Section 5, a substantially complete federal application not decided within 120 days is deemed approved. A federal regulator must evaluate each application, and approved issuers face examination. Before the bill, nonbank stablecoin supervision was primarily at the state level, and OCC rescinded its nonobjection requirement for its supervised institutions in March 2025. Section 5(h) preempts state licensing requirements for federally approved issuers. Sources: [25], [4], [33], [21].

points.title: It enlarges a path from runs on private money to banking stress, disrupted payments, and emergency public support.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It enlarges a path from runs on private money to banking stress, disrupted payments, and emergency public support.

  • Because One dollar of backing does not always mean one safe, available dollar: “the permissible reserve assets include uninsured deposits in banks and shares of credit unions.” [12]
  • Because The bill uses a separate set of loss cushions for issuers: “The bill would require federal and state regulators to issue tailored capital, liquidity, and risk management rules for federal and state stablecoin issuers, but it exempts stablecoin issuers from the regulatory capital standards applied to traditional banks.” [25] Capital is the issuer's own funding available to absorb losses.
  • Because Bank trouble and coin withdrawals can reinforce each other: “Stress at the bank that holds the PPSI’s uninsured deposits could trigger a stablecoin run and a stablecoin run would accelerate the deposit outflow from the already-stressed bank.” [34] PPSI means a permitted issuer; a run means many holders demand cash at once.
  • Because Cashing out also reaches government debt markets. The bill permits Treasury debt “with a remaining maturity of 93 days or less” [4]. BIS reports that “outflows increase yields by two to three times as much as inflows lower them, consistent with the former forcing stablecoin issuers to liquidate their holdings quickly.” [32] This compares the effects of money leaving and entering stablecoins on short-term Treasury interest rates.
  • So A larger, more connected stablecoin market gives mass withdrawals more scope to drain banks and put upward pressure on federal borrowing costs.
  • Because Failure can also freeze payment funds: “The bill would grant stablecoin holders priority over all other claims against the issuer in bankruptcy and would allow a bankruptcy court to issue automatic stays on stablecoin redemptions.” [25] A stay pauses cashing out.
  • Note The faster bankruptcy process still requires a court decision. It directs the court to use “best efforts to enter a final order to begin distributions under this paragraph not later than 14 days after the date of the required hearing.” [4] This gives holders no promise of cash when a payment falls due.
  • Because Reliable access matters beyond investors: “Producers and consumers need to be able to reliably send and receive payments for goods and services bought and sold.” [35]
  • Because A larger role in payments also raises pressure for public rescues. Eichengreen explains the response to a spreading stablecoin panic: “Regulators would feel compelled to step in to prevent the collapse of the payment system.” [35]
  • So Promoting this money puts more ordinary economic activity behind private promises whose failure can spread through banks and markets. It leaves the U.S. government facing payment disruption and pressure for emergency support, threatening national stability and its ability to manage crises.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The researchers cited by the PRO say the Act substantially improves reserve quality and disclosure. Brookings says issuer capital requirements can be lower and simpler than banks' because issuers do not take deposits and lend. The BIS data cover January 2021 to March 2025, before the bill. Sources: [9], [5], [32].

Brief context note: Under Section 5, a substantially complete federal application not decided within 120 days is deemed approved. A federal regulator must evaluate each application, and approved issuers face examination. Before the bill, nonbank stablecoin supervision was primarily at the state level, and OCC rescinded its nonobjection requirement for its supervised institutions in March 2025. Section 5(h) preempts state licensing requirements for federally approved issuers. Sources: [25], [4], [33], [21].

points.title: It risks the credit that sustains U.S. businesses, farms, and communities.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It risks the credit that sustains U.S. businesses, farms, and communities.

  • Because Wider use can “reduce banks’ deposit base as the stablecoin market grows.” [16]
  • Because Losing deposits undermines local loan funding: “The loss of bank deposits will severely impair the ability of community and regional banks to provide much-needed loans to consumers and Main Street businesses.” [36]
  • Because Stablecoin reserves cannot simply replace those loans: “Nonbank stablecoin issuers cannot replace those lost loans because they must invest virtually all their assets in designated short-term financial instruments held as reserves.” [36]
  • Because The shift also leaves behind a lending duty: “Yet unlike deposits at banks, stablecoins have no community lending obligations.” [37]
  • Note The issuer interest ban leaves a way to compete for savings: “GENIUS does not explicitly prevent exchanges from paying rewards on stablecoins held on their exchange” [16].
  • Because Reduced lending reaches employment. The Progressive Policy Institute warns that in many areas “less lending will lead to fewer jobs.” [37]
  • So Shifting savings away from banks that fund local businesses and farms risks scarcer loans, weaker investment, and lost jobs. That weakens the productive communities on which a stable, resilient country depends.
points.con_html:
Response The lending argument leaves out what happens to buyers' money after it reaches an issuer.

  • Because Federal Reserve research explains: “The impact on U.S. bank deposits depends on who demands stablecoins, what assets are converted for stablecoin purchase, and how stablecoin issuers manage reserves.” [38]
  • Because Buying assets other than deposits does not settle the result. The same research says it also depends on “whether counterparties to stablecoin issuers ultimately deposit proceeds back into the banking system.” [38]
  • Because The ban on issuer lending does not stop banks from lending money that returns to them. In its analysis of Treasury-backed reserves, the Council of Economic Advisers explains that “most stablecoin deposits end up redeposited elsewhere in the banking system and able to be lent out.” [39]
  • Because The bill permits a route that preserves a bank's funding: “A bank could issue a stablecoin through a subsidiary, and keep its entire stablecoin reserve balances in demand deposits at its parent bank.” [40]
  • Because The PRO's CRS source says some uses, including foreign remittances and foreigners' savings, are “not likely to cause substitution with U.S. deposits.” [16]
  • So Exchange rewards do not establish where buyers' money comes from or where it ends up. The ban on issuer lending and the absence of issuer community-lending duties do not establish a loss of money local banks can use for loans. The PRO has not shown that the resulting flows reduce local banks' funding or make it costlier or less suited to lending, so its claim of lost local loans and jobs lacks that link.

A federal regulator must evaluate each application, and approved issuers face examination. Section 5(h) preempts state licensing requirements for federally approved issuers. Sources: [25], [4], [33], [21].

points.title: It gives one U.S. state's supervision nationwide reach with only a conditional federal backup.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It gives one U.S. state's supervision nationwide reach with only a conditional federal backup.

  • Because “The bill would permit a nonbank issuer with under $10 billion in outstanding stablecoins to opt in to a state regulatory regime and operate nationally.” [25]
  • Because A federal waiver can keep larger issuers in that system too. Section 4(d)(3) allows an issuer “with a consolidated total outstanding issuance of more than $10,000,000,000 to remain solely supervised by a State payment stablecoin regulator.” [4]
  • Because That makes the resources of the home-state supervisor matter across the country. CRS identifies the concern that state regulators lack “supervisory resources comparable to federal ones.” [2]
  • Because Without an agreement allowing routine Federal Reserve participation, section 7's emergency enforcement route for the Federal Reserve and Comptroller requires “unusual and exigent circumstances” [4] and “not less than 48 hours' prior written notice to the applicable State payment stablecoin regulator” [4]. This backup is a new federal power, so the concern is not that the bill reduces existing federal authority. The concern is that national reach raises the stakes of these limits.
  • Note Certifying that a state's rules are “substantially similar to the Federal regulatory framework under this Act” [4] does not supply equal staffing or remove the federal notice requirement.
  • So A failure of local supervision can expose payments nationwide while the new federal backup faces a delay. Giving national reach to that weak point strains the federal government's ability to contain a fast threat.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Nonbank supervision before the bill was primarily at the state level. Certification of state regimes requires a unanimous federal finding, state and federal regulators must share information, and approved issuers face examination. Sources: [33], [4].

points.title: It makes it easier for commercial platforms to concentrate control over essential payments.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 It makes it easier for commercial platforms to concentrate control over essential payments.

  • Because The bill does not bar commercial ownership of issuers. It does not create this combination of commerce and payments, but its framework makes the route more usable. Its special approval test for publicly traded commercial companies leaves a gap: “privately held nonfinancial companies are not prohibited from issuing stablecoins.” [12] These firms still need an issuer license, but do not face that special test.
  • Because Payment networks become more useful as more people join them, favoring a few large providers: “it is likely there will be only a few stablecoin issuers in a concentrated market.” [12]
  • Because A commercial platform can use its other businesses to strengthen that control: “Serious risks to economic and monetary stability could arise if nonfinancial firms can take advantage of existing private data from their platforms or raise the costs of switching to other payment products.” [12]
  • So The framework makes it easier for firms to build payment systems that become hard to leave, concentrating dependence on their private business choices. Exposing essential payments to that control threatens the stability of U.S. money and payments.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Private firms still need an issuer license, and issuers must have redemption procedures, may not condition service on avoiding competitors, and can be subject to interoperability standards under Section 12. Sources: [4].

points.pro_html:
Point 9 It expands a way for foreign interests to reward a president's business while he directs U.S. policy.

  • Because The president's family already has a stake in this market. Of World Liberty Financial and its USD1 coin, the New Yorker reports that the family “potentially stands to benefit greatly from an expansion in their use.” [41]
  • Because Foreign counterparties can supply that income through the assets backing their coins: “Stablecoins can be lucrative for their issuers, who earn interest on the assets that back them.” [42]
  • Because This channel existed before the vote. Reporting on the May USD1 transaction states that “the investment firm that the UAE founded, MGX, used the stablecoin to purchase a $2 billion stake in Binance.” [42] UAE means United Arab Emirates.
  • Note The bill's ethics clause leaves ownership conflicts open: “Common interpretations of the applicable conflicts of interest statute referenced in the GENIUS Act do not include blanket limitations on ownership of any asset or activity, including an implicit ban on operating a stablecoin.” [28]
  • So Foreign interests can raise income for the president's business by choosing and holding its coin. Expanding that business gives the person directing U.S. policy a private financial reason to please those counterparties. Protecting security decisions from that pressure is part of maintaining a strong U.S. government that serves the country.

points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Bloomberg's July 2025 report describes MGX's use of USD1 for a $2 billion Binance stake and resulting interest income, before the vote. Section 4 preserves applicable ethics statutes. Sources: [42], [4].

pages.reference: Read this value as held by a Christian traditionalist in the United States, with the religious right as the cultural reference. Tradition here concerns preserving, observing or passing down identifiable inherited customs, religious practices and ways of life, valued for their continuity with the past. Religious endorsement of a general moral goal alone does not establish that connection.
pages.description: S.1582 creates federal rules for "stablecoins" — digital coins an issuer must redeem for a fixed dollar value. Only permitted, regulated companies may issue them, and each coin must be fully backed one-to-one by cash or similar safe assets that issuers may not lend out.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.1582?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect S.1582 adds national safeguards for payment stablecoins—digital tokens redeemable for a fixed amount of money. Approved issuers must hold “at least one dollar of permitted reserves for every one dollar of stablecoins issued.” [1] These are assets set aside to repay users. Before the bill, state oversight generally imposed “more limited requirements than the bills propose.” [2]

points.title: It carries the biblical rule of honest dealing into digital payments.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It carries the biblical rule of honest dealing into digital payments.

  • Because Biblical teaching calls for “fair and constant weights and measures in trade” [3].
  • Because Southern Baptist teaching applies Christian duties to public life: “Every Christian should seek to bring industry, government, and society as a whole under the sway of the principles of righteousness, truth, and brotherly love.” [4]
  • Because Alongside full backing, the bill requires issuers to “publish the monthly composition of the issuer's reserves on the website of the issuer” [5].
  • Because Those reports must be “examined by a registered public accounting firm.” [5]
  • Because Issuers must also “disclose in plain language all fees associated with purchasing or redeeming the payment stablecoins” [5].
  • So Backing, checked reports and clear fees make the promised cash value and cost of a token easier to check. Requiring these safeguards applies the inherited rule against false measures to a new form of trade, serving [NAME]'s aim of maintaining that rule.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The CFTC found in 2021 that Tether misrepresented its reserves. Sources: [6].

Evidence note: The monetary-ethics source extends the rule against false weights and measures to stable value in trade; the Baptist statement expressly addresses industry and government. Applying these teachings to stablecoin safeguards is a normative analogy. Neither source specifically endorses this bill, and Christian agreement on the policy is not established. Sources: [3], [4].
points.retirement_reason: Honest weights and sound money are used as general requirements of honest dealing, without a distinct practice or way of life that this legislation helps continue.

points.title: It better protects money given to sustain church life at home and abroad.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It better protects money given to sustain church life at home and abroad.

  • Because Regular giving is an inherited religious duty: “According to the Scriptures, Christians should contribute of their means cheerfully, regularly, systematically, proportionately, and liberally for the advancement of the Redeemer’s cause on earth.” [4]
  • Because Overseas missions are also a religious duty: “The Lord Jesus Christ has commanded the preaching of the gospel to all nations.” [4]
  • Because Stablecoins already provide a way to give. In 2021, the Southern Baptist congregation Back Bay Church offered “USD Coin (USDC) as a donation option.” [7]
  • Because A 2023 international fundraiser for churches in the Philippines also offered stablecoin gifts: “Donors can send Tether (USDT), USD Coin (USDC)” [8]. Coverage depends on the coin: Tether is “licensed in El Salvador” [2], so the rules below for approved issuers reach it only if it becomes one.
  • Because The bill requires issuers to set out “procedures for timely redemption of outstanding payment stablecoins” [5]. Redemption means exchanging a token for money.
  • Because If an approved issuer fails, section 11 gives holders priority over other creditors for required reserves: their claims “shall have priority” [5] “with respect to required payment stablecoin reserves” [5].
  • Because Section 10 also requires firms holding stablecoin reserves for customers to take steps to protect customer property “from the claims of creditors of the person” [5]. Here, “the person” is the firm holding the assets.
  • So For gifts made and held in approved issuers' coins, full backing and stronger rights to recover assets reduce the risk that an issuer's or asset holder's failure takes money intended for Christian work. The sources do not report how long churches hold such gifts as coins.
  • So Protecting these gifts helps congregations sustain worship, teaching and missions. That supports the religious practices [NAME] wants to continue.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Circle reported in 2022 that USDC reserves were held in segregated accounts for holders, with third-party monthly attestations. The cited church and fundraiser reports do not identify custody arrangements or how long gifts stay in coins. Sources: [9], [7], [8].

points.title: It strengthens a way to fight exploitation, carrying an inherited Christian duty into digital finance.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It strengthens a way to fight exploitation, carrying an inherited Christian duty into digital finance.

  • Because Southern Baptist teaching requires care for vulnerable people: “We should work to provide for the orphaned, the needy, the abused, the aged, the helpless, and the sick.” [4]
  • Because Winrock describes trafficked workers forced to run scams: “they commence the work under threat of punishment” [10]. It identifies the payment route: “Cryptocurrency scams utilise USDT” [10].
  • Because Freezing stablecoin funds is a working tool against scams. A June 2025 federal USDT complaint records investigators tracing payments and using other methods to “identify, freeze, and seize the Defendant Property” [11].
  • Because In that case, the U.S. Secret Service asked the issuer for a voluntary freeze: “USSS requested that Tether voluntarily freeze” [11].
  • Because S.1582 requires approved issuers to conduct “monitoring and reporting of any suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation” [5].
  • Because It makes obeying valid federal orders a condition of issuance: “A permitted payment stablecoin issuer may issue payment stablecoins only if the issuer has the technological capability to comply, and will comply, with the terms of any lawful order.” [5]
  • Because Such orders can require an issuer to stop transfers: “prevent the transfer of payment stablecoins issued by the person” [5].
  • Because Sections 3 and 8 also condition U.S. service providers' sales of foreign stablecoins on the issuer having “the technological capability to comply, and will comply, with the terms of any lawful order” [5].
  • So These rules make crime reporting and compliance with freezing orders duties of approved issuers. They also make foreign issuers' compliance with those orders a condition of access through U.S. providers. That adds legal force to a demonstrated way of disrupting scam funds.
  • So Disrupting the money used by scams that exploit trafficked workers helps put the inherited duty to resist abuse into practice. Maintaining that duty gives [NAME] a reason to favor these rules.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO shows that freezes can work, but does not show how the bill’s reporting duties help find the exploitation funds it cites.

  • Because The new foreign-issuer condition concerns compliance with orders, not a new way to locate scam funds. Section 2 requires an order to specify “the payment stablecoins or accounts subject to blocking with reasonable particularity” [5]. The targeted funds must be identified for that tool to work.
  • Because CRS warns that issuers could be “unable to monitor” [2] some illicit uses on public networks where users’ names are hidden. FinCEN's April 2026 proposal likewise states: “FinCEN is not proposing to require a PPSI as part of an AML/CFT program to monitor secondary market activity” [12].
  • So This leaves the duty to obey freezing orders and the condition on foreign issuers unanswered. It challenges the PRO's reliance on reporting duties to find funds moving beyond issuers' own customers. The proposal is not final.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: FinCEN and OFAC's April 2026 proposed rule would apply secondary-market obligations to blocking, freezing and rejecting impermissible transactions and to complying with lawful orders. It does not propose requiring issuers, as part of an AML/CFT program, to monitor secondary-market activity or file SARs on secondary-market transactions, and it requests comment. Section 9(d) rulemaking is separate. Sources: [12].

Evidence note: FinCEN's 2019 guidance applied monitoring and reporting duties to virtual-currency money transmitters. The June 2025 complaint records a November 2023 USSS request for a voluntary Tether freeze. Sources: [13], [11].
points.retirement_reason: The benefit is protection from fraud and forced labor. Christian endorsement of care for vulnerable people adds no distinct Tradition justification.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose S.1582?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect The bill would create a national framework that promotes wider use of payment stablecoins—private digital tokens redeemable for a fixed cash amount. Existing rules are “mainly a diverse set of state money transmitter licensing requirements” [14]. The bill “establishes a regulatory framework for payment stablecoins” [15]. It opens a national route for banks and nonbanks: “Stablecoins could be issued by banks and credit unions (through subsidiaries) or nonbanks.” [1] Clear rules support wider adoption; the White House describes the aim as attracting digital-asset activity by “providing clear rules and promoting responsible innovation in the stablecoin market” [16].

points.title: Required powers to block token spending conflict with an inherited Christian warning about control over buying and selling.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Required powers to block token spending conflict with an inherited Christian warning about control over buying and selling.

  • Because Issuers must have “technical capabilities, policies, and procedures to block, freeze, and reject specific or impermissible transactions that violate Federal or State laws, rules, or regulations” [5].
  • Because That control reaches tokens in users’ own wallets. Steptoe explains that the freeze requirement covers tokens involved in illegal activity, “including tokens held by persons with no relationship to the issuer and regardless of whether the tokens are in a custodial or non-custodial wallet.” [17]
  • Because The bill makes this power a condition of operating. Steptoe states: “However, the GENIUS Act now makes such capabilities a legal prerequisite for operation.” [17]
  • Because Christian Action Network, which is also promoting its own faith-based coin, applies Revelation 13:16–17 to stablecoin control: “The Bible warns that control over buying and selling is the final tool of tyranny.” [18]
  • So Heeding that biblical warning gives [NAME] a reason to resist spreading money whose issuer can stop its use even after it reaches a private wallet.
points.con_html:
Response Making freeze controls compulsory does not establish the religious threat needed to connect this bill to Revelation’s warning.

  • Because The biblical warning concerns exclusion tied to religious allegiance. Thomas Schreiner’s evangelical commentary explains: “No one, no matter his social class or influence, will be able to buy or sell unless he has a mark upon the forehead or hand to signify devotion to the beast.” [19]
  • Because The bill requires coin issuers, the firms that create the tokens, to maintain controls over transactions “that violate Federal or State laws, rules, or regulations” [5]. Its separate definition of a lawful federal freeze order requires that it specify the affected coins or accounts “with reasonable particularity” [5] and be “subject to judicial or administrative review or appeal as provided by law” [5].
  • Because Christian teaching distinguishes legitimate restraint from tyranny. The Southern Baptist Convention states: “Civil government is ordained by God to restrain evil and to promote that which is good” [20].
  • So The reach into private wallets establishes a means of enforcing law. It does not establish religious exclusion or a step toward it. The PRO supplies no link from the bill’s required controls to the religious domination its warning concerns.
points.retirement_reason: The religious allusion labels a financial-control concern but does not identify a religious observance, allegiance requirement or inherited practice the bill impairs.

points.title: Wider use of traceable tokens puts the Christian practice of private giving at risk.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Wider use of traceable tokens puts the Christian practice of private giving at risk.

  • Because The bill requires “identification and verification of account holders with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer” [5] and “monitoring and reporting of any suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation” [5].
  • Because Tracking can follow tokens beyond an issuer’s accounts. Cato explains that “stablecoins can be tracked across a blockchain as they move between holders, even when the transfers happen between wallets that are unhosted by intermediaries” [21]. A blockchain is a shared digital transaction record.
  • Because Cash offers a different form of privacy: “the BSA doesn’t apply when cash changes hands between two people, allowing individuals to transact privately.” [21] The BSA is the Bank Secrecy Act, which requires financial records and reports.
  • Because The PCA Foundation reads Matthew 6 as aimed at giving for recognition: “Jesus’ words weren’t intended to exclude the possibility of any individual outside of ourselves knowing how much we gave, like a church bookkeeper.” [22] It still treats privacy as part of church practice: “We should protect the privacy of our members and their giving.” [22] It says of giving records: “Access should be limited to the smallest number of people possible.” [22] It also describes an existing practice: “People can and do give anonymously to their church.” [22]
  • So Moving gifts from private cash into tokens that can be traced back to identified accounts exposes religious giving to wider scrutiny. Preserving this inherited way of giving gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that shift.
points.con_html:
Response The privacy claim assumes that wider stablecoin use would displace confidential church giving.

  • Because The PCA Foundation’s instruction is to protect giving records: “Access should be limited to the smallest number of people possible.” [22] Its concern includes confidentiality, beyond avoiding public praise.
  • Because The same Christian source identifies ways to preserve the practice: “People can and do give anonymously to their church. They do so either through cash contributions or using a donor-advised fund like those offered by the PCA Foundation.” [22]
  • So Traceability explains the privacy difference between a token transfer and a cash gift. It does not establish that this bill moves church gifts onto a traceable record. The PRO needs that further link to show a threat to the giving practice it identifies.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: FinCEN and OFAC's April 2026 proposed rule would apply secondary-market obligations to blocking, freezing and rejecting impermissible transactions and to complying with lawful orders. It does not propose requiring issuers, as part of an AML/CFT program, to monitor secondary-market activity or file SARs on secondary-market transactions, and it requests comment. Section 9(d) rulemaking is separate. Sources: [12].

points.title: The framework helps online betting businesses receive payments, against a longstanding Christian moral rule.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 The framework helps online betting businesses receive payments, against a longstanding Christian moral rule.

  • Because Payment processor Segpay identifies online gambling as a sector gaining payment opportunities: “For industries like iGaming, adult entertainment, travel, and CBD, the GENIUS Act brings a mix of opportunities and hurdles:” [23]. Here, iGaming means online gambling.
  • Because Segpay explains the benefit of compliant digital dollars as “a pathway to stable and reliable payment processing, removing the risk of being rejected by legacy financial institutions.” [23] Among the hurdles, it says merchants and customers “will have to engage with a financial system that mandates robust Know-Your-Customer (KYC) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) checks.” [23]
  • Because The Southern Baptist Convention affirms its “long-standing history of opposing gambling in its various forms” [24] and calls on government to “curtail sports betting and to address its disastrous effects through policy and legislation” [24].
  • So Helping betting businesses overcome payment barriers, even with those hurdles, works against preserving this religious rule in public life and family habits.
points.con_html:
Response Segpay’s promise of access for betting businesses goes beyond what the bill’s rules for coin issuers establish.

  • Because Gambling payments face separate rules. A Nevada Gaming Lawyer analysis states: “However, casinos must still assess whether such practices are consistent with state licensing rules.” [25] Treasury’s April 2025 account of existing federal rules says covered payment systems must have procedures “reasonably designed to prevent or prohibit restricted transactions.” [26] Those restrictions concern unlawful internet gambling.
  • So Licensing a coin issuer does not approve a betting business or oblige a bank to serve it. This leaves unanswered the clearer payment route Segpay describes for lawful operators. It challenges the claim's reach where these separate gambling rules apply.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Segpay is a payment processor serving these merchants. It describes Tether and USDC as common on online casinos, and it lists challenges including KYC checks, a foreign-issuer barrier and a three-year transition. The Block reported Pornhub accepting USDT in September 2020. Sources: [23], [27].

points.title: Better payment access for pornography businesses conflicts with preserving Christian sexual morals.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Better payment access for pornography businesses conflicts with preserving Christian sexual morals.

  • Because Segpay includes “adult entertainment” [23] among the sectors gaining the payment opportunities above, subject to the same identity-check hurdles.
  • Because Its chief executive explains why alternative payments matter to that trade: “Adult merchants have therefore embraced crypto as a way to tackle our challenges with the banking system.” [28] She identifies the bill’s contribution: “it provides real regulatory clarity.” [28]
  • Because The Southern Baptist Convention teaches that “all production, distribution, and consumption of pornographic material is sin against God, neighbor, and self” [20].
  • So Giving that trade a clearer, more reliable payment route strengthens a business that [NAME]’s tradition teaches families and churches to oppose.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Segpay is a payment processor serving these merchants. It describes Tether and USDC as common on online casinos, and it lists challenges including KYC checks, a foreign-issuer barrier and a three-year transition. The Block reported Pornhub accepting USDT in September 2020. Sources: [23], [27].

points.title: Promoting the payment tools of crypto trading strengthens a pursuit of quick riches that Christian teaching warns families to resist.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Promoting the payment tools of crypto trading strengthens a pursuit of quick riches that Christian teaching warns families to resist.

  • Because Stablecoins already supply money for that market: “Stablecoins are primarily used as payment instruments for speculating in crypto-assets with fluctuating values” [29]. Here, speculation means trading other digital assets in hopes of price gains.
  • Because Focus on the Family applies Proverbs to cryptocurrency speculation: “whoever hastens to be rich will not go unpunished” [30]. It warns against borrowing to seek quick trading profits instead of earning through work or patient investment.
  • So Expanding a payment tool central to that market supports trading built around quick gains. That works against passing on Christian habits of work, patience, and restraint.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: CRS describes the token as issued for payment or settlement and redeemable at a fixed amount. Focus on the Family's warning addresses borrowing to buy crypto or day trading. Sources: [1], [30].
points.retirement_reason: Patience, work and prudence are general virtues here. A contemporary Christian warning against speculation does not identify a custom the bill changes.

points.title: Drawing household money into uninsured tokens puts resources for Christian family duties at risk.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 Drawing household money into uninsured tokens puts resources for Christian family duties at risk.

  • Because The framework promotes tokens that “are not federally insured.” [1]
  • Because The assets issuers must keep to repay token holders do not remove every danger of a rush to cash out. CRS explains that permitted reserve assets are not completely free of risk and concludes that “some run risk would remain.” [2]
  • Because Money can also become unavailable during an issuer’s failure. The bill “would allow a bankruptcy court to issue automatic stays on stablecoin redemptions” [1]—pauses on exchanging tokens for cash.
  • Because Focus on the Family grounds household provision in Paul’s teaching: “if anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” [31].
  • Because For near-term household needs, it teaches: “With short-term investments, the primary goal is liquidity – making sure the money is quickly available to you.” [31]
  • So Families who move insured bank balances into these tokens expose money for household duties to issuer-failure losses and delays. Preserving the inherited duty to provide for one’s family gives [NAME] a reason to oppose promoting that switch.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Uninsured stablecoins were already available, and the bill adds reserve and redemption-procedure duties. CRS's sentence on stays also says the bill would grant holders priority over all other claims against the issuer in bankruptcy. Sources: [14], [5], [1].
points.retirement_reason: The alleged harm is loss of household funds. Describing provision as a religious duty does not establish a distinct inherited family practice affected by that risk.

points.title: Competition for deposits puts lending that supports churches and ministries at risk.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 Competition for deposits puts lending that supports churches and ministries at risk.

  • Because Stablecoin purchases can draw money away from lenders. A Federal Reserve researcher explains that “a sustained migration of these funds into stablecoins reduces the funding available for loan growth unless alternative liabilities are secured.” [32] In plain words, a lender must replace departing deposits to keep funding new loans.
  • Because The bill directs token backing into specified reserves, including “short-dated Treasury bills” [1]. Nonbank issuers cannot simply use those reserves for church loans: “Nonbank stablecoin issuers cannot replace those lost loans because they must invest virtually all their assets in designated short-term financial instruments held as reserves.” [29]
  • Because Deposit-funded ministry lending is an existing Christian practice. Christian Community Credit Union states: “100 percent of the shares are loaned to Christian Community Credit Union members.” [33] Shares are members’ deposits; its accounts include “Loans to Ministry Members” [33].
  • So Drawing deposits away from such lenders threatens funding for churches and ministries. Protecting the institutions through which families practice and pass on their faith gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that pressure.
points.con_html:
Response A conditional bank-funding forecast and a ministry lender’s loan book do not establish that this bill puts ministry lending at greater risk.

  • Because The Federal Reserve researcher states what determines the effect: “The impact on U.S. bank deposits depends on who demands stablecoins, what assets are converted for stablecoin purchase, and how stablecoin issuers manage reserves.” [32]
  • Because The source also distinguishes the funds involved: “Early adoption patterns suggest stablecoins may initially draw more heavily from investment products before significantly impacting core deposits held at banks.” [32] Growth in stablecoins therefore cannot simply be treated as money leaving the deposit pool that funds ministry loans.
  • Because Christian Community Credit Union’s report identifies “Loans to Ministry Members” [33]. That establishes an existing way of funding Christian institutions; it supplies no evidence about how the bill would change its deposits.
  • So The PRO needs a connection between the expected source of stablecoin demand and the funding of lenders serving churches. Its sources do not establish that connection. The gap concerns increased risk to ministry funding, not a missing count of affected churches.

points.title: Expanding a market tied to presidential business interests threatens inherited Christian standards for public service.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 Expanding a market tied to presidential business interests threatens inherited Christian standards for public service.

  • Because The president’s family already had a business in the market when Congress voted. Representative Waters stated on July 17: “The Trump family's crypto company, World Liberty Financial, launched a stablecoin called USD1” [34].
  • Because Stablecoin reserves can earn income for the issuer. The bill permits “short-dated Treasury bills” [1], while “Issuers would be prohibited from paying interest to stablecoin holders.” [1] Wider use therefore expands the earning opportunity for issuers, including the family’s business.
  • Because The bill leaves existing ethics rules in place rather than adding a clear presidential ban. It preserves the “continued application of applicable ethics statutes and regulations administered by the Office of Government Ethics” [5]. CRS explains that “some appear not to apply to a President.” [2]
  • Because Southern Baptist ethicists call for public servants who are “men and women of integrity, principle, and courage” [35]. They connect this to tradition by calling for “a retrieval of the morality and virtue that Adams and Madison believed were prerequisites to the health of our republic” [35].
  • So Growing a business in which the president’s family has a stake enlarges the conflict between public duty and private gain. Preserving the Christian standard that public power serves the public gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that expansion.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: World Liberty Financial's USD1 launched before the vote. Sources: [34].
points.retirement_reason: The objection concerns public integrity and conflicts of interest, rather than preservation or observance of a particular tradition.
